The future of enterprise AI is multi-cloud, multi-model, and dynamically orchestrated. By prioritizing portability and staying close to the market, we haven’t just built a way to use AI – we’ve built a platform that harnesses the best the industry has to offer the moment it arrives. title: [Netflix] Ontology-Driven Observability: Building an End-to-End Knowledge Graph at Netflix Scale
summary: Prasanna Vijayanathan, Renzo Sanchez-SilvaWhen Jake Paul and Mike Tyson stepped into the ring in November 2024, we delivered the fight to roughly 65 million concurrent streams. On an ordinary day our infrastructure takes in more than 2 billion requests and handles upwards of 38 million real-time logging events every second. At that scale, the whole picture doesn’t fit into a single engineering team’s head or onto a single dashboard. With more Live content, Podcasts and real-time streams, our need to understand and update our systems as quickly as possible becomes imperative to provide a good user experience. Understanding the system at this scale and within the time constraints we have, often becomes a daunting exercise in finding a needle in a haystack, in a dark jungle, blindfolded.This post is about that search for the needle.The Four hours before a fixConsider a regression of the kind we see in a given week. The home screen where you see the list of lists of movies, starts taking about 1.5 seconds longer to render. An alert fires. And then we go looking for what caused this issue and how do we fix it?As it so happens, a regression on the application could be related to anywhere in the system — a client app regression from a new version deployment or A/B test rollout, a load shedding in the infrastructure, a GraphQL query responding with bad data because of a service rollout 6 hops downstream, are all suspects at this point. So, answering “what caused the issue?” needs insights from across the system, and this involves combing through layers of data in a meticulous manner.The MELT Layer“What caused the issue?”Metrics, events, logs and traces, or MELT, in the industry’s shorthand, are the right raw materials for such an investigation, and each of them answers roughly a quarter of the question. We collect observability data across these four pillars, unified into a single observability data layer. This lets us observe our systems in real time, across what our users are experiencing, how our applications are doing and what our backend infrastructure and services are processing and responding to.MELT — Metrics, Events, Logs and Traces, and how they are captured across the system.The investigation that follows may look like this in each layer:What each layer of MELT tells us and what it leaves outThe timeline of an investigationSo how long does it take to investigate an issue, figure out the root cause and fix it, so our users stop running into this issue again?A timeline of an investigation: ~4 hoursIn our chosen example, four hours. Very little of it went into computing anything difficult. Most of it went into reconstructing relationships that our observability systems already knew but we had never written down anywhere a human or machine could simply read and discover.The disagreement underneathThe instinct here could have been, around 2023, to reach for more data or better dashboards, and while both help at the margins, neither addresses what makes these investigations slow.It’s 2026 now, so we might say, “hey, agents”, but without the right context delivered to the agents, AI systems hallucinate, and especially when teams are on-call and need a fix “now”, we cannot let inaccurate agentic analysis lead us down the wrong path. We need the right needle, not any needle.Each of our systems is internally coherent and externally isolated. Atlas, our telemetry platform, knows applications and their time series. Radar, our alerting system, knows thresholds and firing history. incident.io knows severities and responders. PagerDuty knows rotations. Spinnaker knows what shipped and when. And our Slack history knows, in a form no query engine can reach, which engineer solved something very similar last quarter and what they found.The difficulty is that they do not agree on what they are talking about. A thing that is an application in one system is a service in a second and a cluster in a third, with names differing by a suffix, a casing convention, or a rename only a couple of people remember (SMEs, ring a bell?). Joining across them requires a human carrying the mapping in their head, and that person becomes the bottleneck in such cross-domain investigations. The hard part of end-to-end observability is probably better understood as a data modelling problem.What we lacked was an explicit, machine-readable agreement about the entities in our operational world.The OntologyThis agreement has a name: an ontology. Ontology is a formal specification of types, the properties they carry, and the relationships they may have. Its unit is the triple, one fact expressed as subject, predicate, object. Consider the following example triples.api-gateway rdf:type ops:Application .api-gateway ops:ownedBy "Team Bedrock" .api-gateway ops:deployedIn "us-east-1" .INC-5377 rdf:type ops:Incident .INC-5377 ops:affects api-gateway .INC-5377 ops:severity "SEV 2" .In the example here, we have already encoded six facts, and can answer in one query, a question that used to span three tools.“Which incidents affected applications owned by Team Bedrock in us-east-1?” is a single query in place of looking up incidents, Spinnaker and Radar.We call our ontology layer, The Observability Ontology. It acts as the schema, rule set and shared agreement that standardizes how different systems understand entities like applications, services, incidents, deployments, etc.We built it on the W3C stack for this: RDF for the data model, OWL for the ontology, SHACL for validation, and SPARQL for querying. These standards are well specified and widely implemented, which keeps the model portable across graph stores.The data from the ontology itself, is stored as a knowledge graph, persisted to QuipuDB, our homegrown RDF graph database, a distributed quad store based on redb, a Rust-based embedded key value db. Data here is generated by parsing raw telemetry, logs, and incident discussions into triples (subject-predicate-object facts).Every harvest also produces a full Turtle serialization for archival, making it human-readable and diff-friendly, which has proven more useful for debugging than we expected.Our ontology is organized into twelve namespaces, each owning one operational domain:There are two decisions about this ontology that mattered while we built it, so they’re worth sharing.The first is that we refused a generic Service type. “Service” means four different things across our tooling, so applications resolve to exactly one type, ops:Application, and every one of them is validated against our software catalog of roughly 49,000 entries before the entity is created. Unvalidated strings like usernames, team names, dependency names scraped from network topology, never become applications. We also cap dependency edges in both directions, because one popular service can carry thousands of reverse dependencies and would otherwise dominate the graph.The second decision concerns what we chose to model. Incident chat carries the reasoning behind an incident. The hypotheses tried and discarded, the mitigation that worked, who knew why, is all context in the incident’s Slack channel and that knowledge evaporates when the channel goes quiet. So a 200-message, 50-person, 15-service incident channel becomes a structure, converting the operational chaos of an incident into ordered triples:Creating determinism from non-determinismBuilding this graph means using tools that are inherently stochastic. LLMs summarize discussions. Fuzzy matching resolves service names. A probabilistic engine proposes causal chains. None of these produce the same output twice with certainty, but what comes out at the end of our system is a deterministic graph that answers a SPARQL query the same way every time.The ontology is the mechanism that creates this determinism through its pipelined approach. We think of the pipeline as a ladder that drives entropy down, where entropy means the proportion of information still trapped in unstructured form. For example, at the start of this pipeline, an LLM could say anything, but it cannot emit a triple that violates the type system. We constrain the output space tightly enough and a stochastic process yields a deterministic contract:# The model may produce any prose. Its output MUST fit these predicates:category IN sentiment IN # Result — a deterministic triple:thread:123 slack:category "incident" .thread:123 slack:isIncidentRelated "true"^^xsd:boolean .There are five layers that get us down this ladder. Any single step of this ladder is non-deterministic. But in aggregate, the chain becomes deterministic. That inversion is the whole trick. We describe them below:The five layers to create determinism from non-determinismEnrichers: Agents as entropy reducersWe use what we call, enrichers, to reduce entropy across the knowledge graph. Dozens of enrichers run over the graph. Each one of them takes noisy input and emits typed triples, and each reads what earlier enrichers wrote. The contract for an Enricher is deliberately narrow:class Enricher: async def _enrich_async(self, ...): raw = await self.fetch(...) # 1. read noisy input result = self.analyze(raw) # 2. process (may be stochastic) graph.add((uri, RDF.type, OPS.X)) # 3. emit TYPED triples graph.add((uri, OPS.pred, Literal(result.value))) return EnrichmentResult(success=True, triples_added=count)Three invariants that are standard across the enrichers:every entity carries an rdf:type,every URI follows a single naming scheme, andthe catalog gates every ops:Application.Two operational choices are worth naming here, as well. The enrichment pipeline runs sequentially — load the graph, add triples, and save.This sequencing removes an entire category of race conditions at a cost in wall-clock time we are happy to pay. And calls out to external systems like metrics, logs, events and the rest could be best-effort, so a slow downstream API doesn’t block the graph harvest, albeit some degradation. To that end, we are also working to translate these separate systems into the ontology, such as the Metrics Ontology and the Alerts Ontology, so everything could be queried from the Ontology itself.The Correlation Engine: finding the correlation chainsThe correlation engine assimilates the vast number of signals from diverse input sources and condenses them into causal or correlatory chains of events. Today, the engine reads thirteen signal types, including log errors, metric anomalies, slow and failed traces, alerts, incidents, deployments, config changes, experiments, autoscaling, commits, end-to-end bottlenecks, and error patterns. It then searches for paths among them. Some ordered pairs are known to be causal and carry a high prior weight. For example, deployment before log error, config change before metric anomaly, failed trace before incident, and so on. Others, which show high correlation are considered correlation chains. Such chains are scored on temporal proximity and severity, inside a ten-minute window, with anything under 0.6 confidence getting discarded.The Correlation EngineThe role of the engine here is to propose with evidence, not to make conclusions. Hence, the engine stores its chains along with the graph records that were used to create them.A 0.87 chain in the above example, is a strong hypothesis for a human or an agent to check, and the graph records the confidence alongside the claim so that consumers can understand why a chain is what it is and weigh their options to make decisions.The knowledge flywheelEach harvest cycle turns the same four steps, and each rotation leaves the graph richer for the next. This is the Knowledge Flywheel, leading to continuous enrichment and improvement of the context about our system, stored in the knowledge graph.The Knowledge FlywheelObserve collects the signals. Enrich adds typed triples. Infer finds patterns invisible in the raw data. Adapt feeds knowledge back, so that established patterns become detection rules. The compounding result of the four phases leads to a self-improving system. A causal chain discovered in one incident becomes a known pattern for the next, and the ontology gradually stops being a schema and starts being a memory.Consider the example above. When we first see an incident in api-gateway caused due to a timeout and resolve it, we convert this knowledge into entries to the ontology. This becomes encoded knowledge. As we go through multiple cycles of this encoding, the graph starts learning patterns. After N cycles, patterns become wisdom — “api-gateway deploys cause 40% of SEV-2s” and “30% of deployment issues in api-gateway come from Connection Timeouts”. Surface this as an insight and we proactively start reducing incidents, not just react quickly to new ones.Putting the graph to workOn top of the graph sits AutoRCA, our internal agentic AI solution, built with a set of specialist agents coordinated around one question. Walking the home page regression from the top of this post, the agentic system’s reasoning chain might look something like this:Each specialization to the inputs is built by people who understand their respective domain deeply. That division of labour only works if the specialists can pass findings to one another without having to agree on the terms of communication or even have knowledge of each other. The ontology acts as the interface. Each specialist learns one vocabulary — the graph’s. A team writing specialized use cases for how they use traces record their findings as triples about an ops:Application, the logs specialization reads triples about that same ops:Application, and neither needs to know the other exists. A new specialist learns the same vocabulary once and can immediately read everything the other six have written.Set against the investigation we opened with, the change is narrower than it might sound. The alert still fires at 3:30pm, an engineer still has to weigh the evidence, and the fix still has to be written by someone who understands the code. The hour or two that used to go into assembling context — finding the owning team, reconstructing what shipped, correlating information from different parts of the system, recalling that something similar happened last quarter — all that work is the part the ontology and the graph absorbs. We are early enough that the ranked hypotheses are sometimes wrong, which is why each one carries the evidence that produced it. But when the engineer now starts the investigation, they are already holding the picture that used to take half an afternoon to assemble.If you want to build one of theseA fair amount of what we have built, we learned by getting it wrong first. Based on this experience, these are the principles we would carry into a second attempt.Model identity before anything else. Choose one authoritative catalog per entity kind and validate against it before creating an entity.Treat the ontology as code. Version it, review it, test it, and let changes arrive as pull requests. Treating the ontology as code lends itself to agentic development and lets teams scale and contribute to it.Separate concepts from instances. Concepts change on a human timescale and instances change continuously, conflating them makes both harder to evolve.Build on open standards. RDF, OWL, SHACL and SPARQL are specified, implemented many times over, and portable. A bespoke graph model ties a future consumer to one implementation.Constrain stochastic tools with a type system. This is the principle we would defend hardest. Models are useful precisely where determinism is impossible, and a sufficiently narrow output contract converts their output into something a query engine can trust.Make enrichment best-effort and ordered. A slow dependency should utmost degrade the graph, never block it. And ordering enrichers so each builds on the last buys more accuracy and that’s worth the tradeoff with parallelism that buys speed.Model human reasoning alongside machine telemetry. The most valuable edges in our graph came from discussion. Telemetry records what the system did, discussion records what people understood and interpreted. The reasoning is more valuable to store and serve as wisdom when we need it.Keep humans as the approvers. Let agents propose fixes, enrichers, and ontology changes, and route every proposal through a review process with humans in the loop.What comes nextThe graph makes three things possible. First, automatic root cause analysis, where a regression arrives with a ranked set of graph-backed hypotheses attached. Next, automated remediation, where a sufficiently confident diagnosis carries a proposed action like a targeted rollback, a traffic shift, a code change. And eventually infrastructure that heals itself, acting on a predicted failure before members feel it.Alongside this, we plan to integrate the Observability Ontology with Upper, the domain-modeling language at the heart of Netflix’s Unified Data Architecture (UDA). Upper lets teams describe business and system domains as interconnected, machine-readable models and preserve their meaning and constraints as those models are projected into concrete schemas and systems. This integration would connect operational concepts such as applications, alerts, deployments, and incidents to the broader set of domains modeled across Netflix, giving engineers and agents a shared semantic layer for querying, validation, and reasoning. We will begin with a proof of concept that models incidents in Upper and use what we learn to determine where the two systems should converge.AcknowledgementsNone of this would exist without the teams who share their data, expertise, and patience with an early system. We want to specially acknowledge the efforts of our own team members who made this possible from very early on in this lifecycle, Kaela Marsheck and Aditya Gaur. We are also especially grateful to our collaborators in Netflix’s ontology working group, Peter Royal, Alex Hutter, and to Alexandre Bertails and members of the Unified Data Architecture (UDA)/Knowledge Foundations team for sharing Upper and their domain-modeling expertise, and for helping us explore how the Observability Ontology can become part of a broader semantic foundation at Netflix.Ontology-Driven Observability: Building an End-to-End Knowledge Graph at Netflix Scale was originally published in Netflix TechBlog on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: [Microsoft Azure] Designing for sovereign AI: A shared foundation from edge to cloud
summary: As organizations apply AI to more business-critical and data-intensive workloads, AI processing is moving closer to where data is created, decisions are made, and operations take place. Manufacturers can analyze confidential production data next to the systems that generate it. Pharmaceutical companies can apply AI to clinical trials within controlled environments. Government agencies can run AI applications on sensitive information while maintaining established security and operational boundaries. This shift reflects ongoing innovation across the technology ecosystem to give organizations greater flexibility in where they run AI and process sensitive data, and it is changing the digital sovereignty conversation. It now encompasses where data is stored and processed, where workloads run, who can access and operate the systems around them, and how those systems remain secure and operational as requirements change. The next phase of digital sovereignty will take shape across the technology ecosystem, through closer alignment among silicon, infrastructure, cloud, security, data, and AI. Learn more about digital sovereignty As AI extends into more sensitive and mission-critical workloads, sovereignty must be designed across the stack, from silicon and infrastructure to cloud, data, and AI. Microsoft and Intel® are working together to help organizations create a more consistent foundation for innovation, while retaining greater choice over where workloads run and how they are controlled. A flexible sovereign architecture allows organizations to place each workload in the right environment, apply the controls it requires, and maintain a more consistent technology and operating foundation as requirements evolve. Sovereignty must work across the technology stack Sovereignty requirements vary by workload. The right level of control depends on factors such as data sensitivity, regulation, latency, connectivity, operational access, and resilience requirements. This creates a continuum, where organizations can apply different levels of control across public cloud, customer-controlled environments, and trusted partner solutions. Delivering that flexibility requires the underlying technology layers to work together. The controls that shape where a workload runs, how data is protected, who can access it, and how the environment is verified extend across silicon, infrastructure, cloud, security, data, and AI. This is where the Microsoft and Intel partnership comes into focus. Together, we are working to create a more consistent foundation across these layers, giving organizations greater choice in where workloads run and how they are controlled. This principle is central to the work between Microsoft and Intel. Azure Local, running on Intel® Xeon® 6 processors, brings distributed Azure infrastructure together with a common compute foundation for customer-controlled environments. Organizations can extend cloud and AI capabilities closer to their data and operations while maintaining consistent approaches to security, management, and governance. Trust must be designed for and verified For sensitive workloads, trust must be supported by technical protections and verifiable evidence. Organizations need to protect workloads across the technology stack and verify that systems are operating under the security conditions they have established. That starts at the compute layer and extends through identity, encryption, governance, policy, and operations. For supported Azure Confidential VM configurations, Intel® Xeon® processors provide hardware-based protections, including Intel® Trust Domain Extensions (Intel TDX), which can help isolate workloads while they are in use. Hardware-backed attestation can provide evidence that helps organizations verify relevant security properties of the environment against their requirements. Microsoft extends this foundation through security and governance controls across cloud and customer-controlled environments. Together, these capabilities can help organizations verify relevant security properties of the environment against their requirements. This is particularly important as AI brings regulated, proprietary, and mission-critical data into new workloads. Each workload should receive protections proportionate to its risk. Isolation, encryption, attestation, and operational controls can be applied where they provide meaningful value while preserving a manageable operating model across the broader environment. Digital sovereignty requires trust across the technology stack. Together, Intel and Microsoft are combining hardware-based security and confidential computing with cloud, AI and distributed infrastructure to help customers protect sensitive workloads and verify the environments in which they run. This shared foundation gives organizations greater control, confidence and choice, with the performance and scale to continue innovating as AI moves into more regulated and mission-critical environments. —Anand Pashupathy, Vice President and General Manager, Intel Product Assurance and Security Sovereign AI brings intelligence closer to data Much of the data with the greatest potential for AI must remain within defined operational, regulatory, or security boundaries. This includes data tied to industrial operations, government services, clinical environments, intellectual property, and proprietary research. Workload placement has therefore become a practical AI decision. Organizations need the flexibility to run AI closer to their data, applications, and operations. Delivering that flexibility requires infrastructure, cloud platforms, AI software, and security capabilities to work as a connected foundation. Microsoft Foundry helps organizations build and deploy AI applications and models, with options for where AI runs based on their requirements. Foundry Local enables organizations to run AI inference in their own environments, closer to the data and applications those models rely on. On the same infrastructure, Intel Xeon 6 processors with Intel® Advanced Matrix Extensions (Intel AMX) can accelerate AI workloads directly on the CPU. Intel® OpenVINO™ helps developers optimize and deploy models across supported infrastructure. This approach extends across the broader application environment. Organizations may need to manage AI, applications, data, development, and productivity workloads within the same governance and operational boundary. Microsoft 365 Local and GitHub Enterprise Local extend customer-controlled options to collaboration, source code, and software development workflows. Sovereign AI brings models, data, applications, development tools, and infrastructure together under the controls each workload requires. This approach allows organizations to apply AI within the operational and governance boundaries established for their most sensitive data. Organizations want to apply AI to their most valuable data while maintaining the controls that data requires. On supported Azure confidential VM configurations, Intel TDX helps make that possible by running AI workloads in hardware-isolated trust domains, protecting models and data while in use and isolating them from the host and hypervisor. Hardware-backed attestation then gives organizations evidence they can check against their own requirements, so they can move from trusting their environment to verifying it. —Anand Pashupathy, Vice President and General Manager, Intel Product Assurance and Security Sovereignty architecture must be adaptable Sovereignty requirements will continue to change. A workload that runs in a connected environment today may face different regulatory, resilience, or connectivity requirements tomorrow. AI models, applications, and infrastructure will also continue to evolve. A sovereign architecture must therefore provide control without creating rigidity. Organizations should be able to adapt where workloads run, how they are secured, and how they connect without rebuilding their management and security model each time requirements change. This is another reason partnership across the technology stack matters. Alignment across silicon, infrastructure, cloud, security, and AI software can give organizations a more stable foundation even as individual technologies and workload requirements evolve. A well-designed sovereign architecture gives organizations room to respond as regulations, technologies, and operating conditions change. Explore Microsoft Sovereign Cloud in Europe Discover how Microsoft Sovereign Cloud in Europe helps organizations address evolving data sovereignty, security, and compliance requirements while accelerating cloud and AI innovation. Learn more Three questions leaders should ask Digital sovereignty can become abstract quickly. A better place to start is the workload. 1. What must remain under your control? Consider the data, infrastructure, administrative access, software operations, and connectivity on which the workload depends. The answer may differ by application, even within the same organization. 2. Can you verify that those controls are working? Policies and contractual commitments are important, but sensitive workloads may also require technical evidence. Consider how your architecture supports encryption, isolation, identity and access control, policy enforcement, attestation, and operational transparency. 3. Will the architecture leave you room to adapt? AI capabilities, regulations, operating conditions, and workload requirements will continue to change. Your architecture should allow you to adopt new models, move processing closer to data, and adjust where workloads run without creating an entirely separate technology environment each time. Digital sovereignty depends on cloud, infrastructure, security, AI, and silicon working together. Our collaboration with Intel gives customers a more consistent foundation across these layers, so they can apply stronger controls where needed while retaining the flexibility to innovate. —Bernardo Caldas, CVP, Azure Edge Product Management The strongest sovereignty strategy preserves choice Digital sovereignty should give organizations greater control over the technology and data they depend on while preserving their capacity to innovate. Achieving that outcome requires collaboration across the technology ecosystem. Microsoft and Intel are connecting silicon, infrastructure, cloud, security, and AI to give organizations greater flexibility in where workloads run, how they are protected, and how they evolve. A shared foundation across these layers allows organizations to apply the right controls to each workload and benefit from advances across the broader technology ecosystem. A strong sovereignty strategy meets today’s requirements while preserving tomorrow’s options. Resources to learn more Dive deeper into digital sovereignty to learn how Microsoft is helping organizations address data residency, operational control, security, and regulatory requirements across cloud and customer-controlled environments. Learn more about Microsoft Sovereign Private Cloud. Join us at Microsoft Ignite in November to hear the latest on Microsoft Sovereign Cloud, Azure Local, AI, security, and infrastructure innovation. title: [Docker] Security Update on PHP2Shell: Impact for Docker Customers
summary: Summary On Tuesday, October 20, 2026, Docker began tracking two critical vulnerabilities in PHP, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, commonly known as PHP2Shell. The vulnerabilities allow attackers to execute code remotely in PHP core, and they affect PHP packages going back to version 5.4: the supported versions 8.2 through 8.5, and the end-of-life versions 5.x, 7.x, 8.0, and 8.1. To address these vulnerabilities, PHP released 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35, and advised anyone running PHP to update to the latest version immediately. Although this is a vulnerability in PHP itself, not in Docker’s systems, it nonetheless affects Docker users who build on PHP images and packages. In response, we have updated the Docker Hardened Images and Docker Official Images on Docker Hub, and advise customers to immediately update. What Happened Along with other package repositories and secure package providers, Docker has been made aware of and is tracking two recently discovered critical vulnerabilities in PHP packages distributed since version 5.4. The two critical vulnerabilities, now commonly referred to as “PHP2Shell,” are identified and tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. (The PHP Foundation has published a detailed report on the discovery that we recommend reading for full context.) In short: these vulnerabilities could allow remote code execution in PHP core by malicious actors. Both are flaws in how PHP manages request memory. In CVE-2026-109618, when PHP runs out of memory mid-request and aborts, some code paths leave memory uninitialized, and PHP’s cleanup step then reads it. In CVE-2026-109619, PHP’s internal state can keep pointing at memory that has already been freed, and a later request then uses that stale state. Attackers have multiple ways to trigger either condition and turn it into remote code execution. Affected versions include the currently supported versions (8.2 through 8.5), as well as the EOL and unsupported versions 5.x, 7.x, 8.0, and 8.1. Impact to Anyone Using PHP Whether you are a Docker user or not, if you are using any of the above affected versions of PHP, you should immediately upgrade to the latest version. That includes PHP 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27, or 8.5.12, or a later release in the corresponding branch. There is no other comprehensive remediation for the affected versions. Updating is the only complete mitigation path. If for any reason you are unable to complete an immediate update, we strongly recommend taking your system offline until such time that you can initiate mitigation. This the guidance of not only Docker, but of the FBI, and numerous experts throughout the cybersecurity community. Impact to and Actions for Docker Users While this vulnerability exists in PHP itself and not directly in Docker’s systems, there is nonetheless potential risk and exposure to Docker customers who run PHP in their applications, including anyone using PHP images or packages from Docker Hub, Docker Official Images, or Docker Hardened Images. For users of Docker Official Images:Docker Official Images have already been updated and released to Docker Hub and mirrored to Amazon ECR. Customers using either of these sources should update immediately. For users of Docker Hardened Images (DHI):Docker Hardened Images have already been updated and released to Docker Hub. The currently supported versions of PHP were updated as follows: 8.2.34 → 8.2.35 8.3.35 → 8.3.36 8.4.26 → 8.4.27 8.5.11 → 8.5.12 The updates to our images were completed and released within 24-hours of the upstream patches being made available. These images were made available after successfully executing the DHI testing and verification processes. What’s next If you have any issues accessing the updated images or migrating to the new versions, please contact Docker Support at app.docker.com/support/contact. As always when it comes to matters of security, we appreciate your diligence.

title: [Red Hat] Why ITOps needs a governed automation foundation for AI
summary: Lately I hear many customers saying the same thing in different words—they added an AI layer to their environment, expected everything to get better, but haven't really noticed anything different yet.In practice, the addition I see first usually sits upstream, whether that's a copilot, an AIOps correlation layer, or an agent able to reason across tools. title: [Amazon AWS] AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities is now generally available
summary: Today, we’re announcing the general availability of AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities. AWS Continuum is a security service that finds and validates code vulnerabilities, then delivers fixes as patches you can automate or as pull requests in your repositories. AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities confirms which findings are exploitable in your environment, ranks the resulting issues by business impact, and proposes a fix for each one. Every remediation starts in a mode where Continuum proposes the fix and a person approves it before it ships. In the future, you will be able to decide which actions Continuum can take on its own, within the guardrails you define. Using frontier artificial intelligence (AI) models, threat actors can turn a vulnerability disclosure into working exploit code in minutes, and the same tools that speed up development also increase the volume of findings your teams must process. If your organization runs a large application estate, your scanners likely produce thousands of findings a day, and many of them need no action. A finding can be unreachable, unexploitable, or already mitigated by a runtime control. Generic severity scores don’t tell you which resources a threat actor can actually reach, so a critical score on a dev-only utility looks the same as a medium score on a service one step away from a payments database. Previously, confirming whether a finding was exploitable took hours of manual investigation, and shipping a fix with confidence took days of coordination across security, infrastructure, and application teams, because the blast radius of a change is hard to assess without business context. To close that gap, Continuum proves which findings are exploitable and bounds the risk of each fix it proposes. Continuum builds a context graph from two primary sources: your code repositories and your AWS environment. For AWS, you set up a collector in the account and Region where your code runs. The collector gathers resource details such as AWS Config resources and network configuration so Continuum can judge whether a vulnerability is reachable over the network and what a threat actor could reach from it. From this graph, Continuum learns which systems are business-critical, who owns them, how services depend on one another, and which data each one touches. It uses that picture to identify your highest-value systems, such as customer data stores, payment pipelines, and authentication services, and then ranks each resulting issue by how close its attack path runs to those systems. Continuum analyzes each finding against your code and its environment context and assigns an evidence level, such as a verdict proven by static analysis of the vulnerable code path. For findings it can reproduce, Continuum runs the exploit in an isolated sandbox and attaches proof-of-concept code with the reproduction steps. It produces the attack path, the supporting source analysis, and a blast radius assessment instead of a risk score alone. It also evaluates whether your existing defenses would detect and stop the validated path. For each confirmed issue, Continuum generates a fix (a code patch, a dependency upgrade, or a configuration change) and opens it as a pull request in your connected repository, ready to review. Every fix requires human approval: you review and merge the pull request, so the final decision stays with your team. In the future, you will be able to build confidence in specific remediation classes and let Continuum apply those fixes automatically once its confidence gates pass, such as test coverage, scope bounds, and historical success rate. AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities in action To show how this works, I open AWS Continuum in the console and go to Code vulnerabilities. Before I can review issues, I set up an environment. I connect a code source, either a GitHub integration or an Amazon S3 bucket, and then create an environment that scans it on a schedule I choose. An Amazon S3 source has a couple of prerequisites: the bucket sits in the same account and AWS Region where I turn on AWS Continuum, and I grant access through an AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role that AWS Continuum assumes. I can optionally add AWS infrastructure context by setting up an AWS Continuum collector in the account and Region where my code runs and authorizing my environment to use it. For the full requirements and steps, see the AWS Continuum User Guide. The Overview page brings these pieces together in one place, showing my Code integrations, the Environments built on them, and the status of any AWS collector that supplies AWS resource context. I open one of my environments. The Issues tab lists validated, prioritized issues rather than raw scanner output, each with a severity, a status, and the time it was created. I choose one of the issues. The Overview rates it High severity, with the status Completed and the remediation already Delivered to GitHub. The Risk assessment explains why. Continuum rates its Exploitability as Exploitable, with an evidence level of Static proven and a validation run status of Completed. Likelihood is High, since the service is reachable from an attacker, requires no authentication, and needs no user interaction. Impact is Moderate, which means an attacker gains the ability to modify business data, with a blast radius reaching other users in the same tenant. A Proof section includes the source analysis behind the verdict. The Remediation section shows a fix already delivered as a pull request in GitHub, changing four files, with 50 lines added and 24 removed across the cart service. Continuum opens the fix as a pull request titled Continuum fix, and I choose View pull request to open it in GitHub. The console is explicit that a generated patch does not mean the issue is fixed. I still review and merge it, which keeps the final decision with my team. A Contributing findings section lists the specific scanner finding this issue was built from. The pull request description carries the same risk assessment, remediation summary, and proof from the console, so whoever reviews it in GitHub sees the evidence without leaving their workflow. The Findings tab lists the raw scanner findings across the environment, the evidence that issues are built from. The Scans tab shows the history of each scan with its status, origin, and request and completion times, and I use Configure scan frequency to change the cadence or Queue scan to run one on demand. The Configuration tab is where I manage the environment: the code and context sources it reads from, its code integrations, environment settings such as whether Continuum creates remediation patches, and the AWS collectors it uses for AWS context. In a single workflow, I work through the validated issues in priority order with each scan, reviewing the evidence and scope behind each one before I approve and merge the fixes I trust. Every fix waits for my approval, so the backlog keeps shrinking while my team keeps control of what ships. Now available AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities is available today in US East (N. Virginia) and US West (Oregon) Regions. For pricing, visit the pricing page. To learn more, visit the AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities product page and the User Guide. Give it a try in the AWS Continuum console today, and send us feedback through your usual AWS Support contacts. — Esra

title: [HashiCorp] Secure AI agents with HashiCorp Boundary
summary: Locally running cowork and coding AI agents are evolving from passive assistants into active participants in enterprise IT operations -analyzing logs, investigating incidents, assessing system health, and recommending next steps. While this can accelerate troubleshooting and reduce operational toil, enterprise adoption requires answering a critical question beyond improving productivity: How can an AI agent interact with infrastructure without creating new security, compliance, or governance risks? This blog explores how to leverage HashiCorp Boundary’s zero trust access model to provide AI agents with secure, governed access to infrastructure resources. To explore this challenge in practice, we used IBM technologies and services to create an AI agent that runs on developer workstation and is capable of investigating infrastructure incidents through natural-language requests. For example, a platform engineer can ask the agent to analyze a performance issue, gather diagnostic data from a target system, and summarize the findings. The key objective was not only to build an AI agent but to ensure that every infrastructure interaction remained secure, controlled, and auditable. The solution overview The AI agent enables a platform engineer to describe an operational goal in natural language: A sample prompt can be: “Investigate memory pressure on app-server-01 and summarize the findings.” The following diagram shows the architecture and workflow for an AI agent built with IBM Bob. The AI agent uses watsonx and Granite models to interpret an operational request, develop an investigation plan, execute the required diagnostic actions, analyze the results, and produce a concise summary for the platform engineer. When infrastructure access is required, the AI agent running on the platform engineer workstation initiates a login to Boundary, and the platform engineer completes the authentication on behalf of the agent. The AI agent then opens a Boundary-proxied session to the authorized Linux target to perform the investigation. Session activity is recorded, and audit logs capture authentication events, access decisions, grants, policy changes, and administrative actions. This creates a human-authorized workflow for an AI-assisted operation without relying on fully unattended infrastructure access. The zero trust layer As shown in the architecture diagram, Boundary provides the secure access layer between the AI agent and the target infrastructure. Rather than granting the agent direct access to systems, Boundary evaluates the authenticated user's identity, permissions, and target access policies before establishing a connection. This separation of access control from AI reasoning ensures that infrastructure access remains governed by enterprise security policies. Secure access with Boundary In this model, Boundary enables five essential controls: Identity-based authentication: Boundary delegates authentication to IBM Verify through an OIDC authentication method and applies access policies to the verified identity. Zero trust connectivity: The agent reaches the target only through an active Boundary session, without requiring the agent host to have a direct network route or VPN access to the target’s private network. Boundary workers proxy the connection to the target. Target grants: Least-privilege grants restrict network access to only the Linux targets required for the agent’s operational task. Secrets management: Vault stores or generates target credentials, including short-lived dynamic credentials. Boundary retrieves and injects the credentials when it establishes the session, without returning them to the agent or platform engineer. This ensures credentials are shared, leaked, stolen, or insecurely stored. Administrative control: Authorized administrators can cancel an active session, providing a kill switch for infrastructure access. Auditability and session recording Boundary captures the agent’s infrastructure activity within the same governed access layer used for human operators. Session recordings provide visibility into session interactions and the associated target, user, host, and connection metadata. Boundary also emits audit events for authenticated requests, session activity, and administrative operations. Together, session recording and audit events provide centralized evidence for incident reviews, security investigations, and compliance validation, helping organizations treat the AI agent as a controlled and auditable participant in enterprise operations. Demo The video demonstrates how an AI agent uses a Platform Engineer’s verified identity and permissions to access enterprise resources through Boundary with governance and auditability. Final thoughts As AI agents move from analysis to infrastructure action, enterprises must embed security, governance, and accountability directly into the workflow. Automation alone is not enough; organizations also need controls that govern identity, access, credentials, sessions, and evidence. In this example, we used watsonx.ai to support the agent’s reasoning, planning, and summarization; Boundary to authorize and proxy infrastructure access; Verify to authenticate the platform engineer; and Vault to manage and inject target credentials. Together, these technologies create a secure, governed model for agent-assisted enterprise operations. The agent can help perform infrastructure tasks while operating within the identity, access, session, and audit controls expected from human operators. Building the AI agent You can try testing this workflow out in your environment. There are several possible approaches, but you can build your AI agent and enable secure access to your resources using Boundary by setting up the services and accounts as described below: IBM Cloud and watsonx.ai: Create an IBM Cloud account and use watsonx.ai python SDK to build the agent. IBM watsonx.ai provides access to the foundation models and tools that an AI agent can use for reasoning, planning, and summarization. You can also use IBM Bob, an agentic development partner, to design and implement the AI agent through natural-language prompts. Alternatively, you can use the AI agentic frameworks of your choice to develop your AI agent. Linux host or cloud VM: Create a Linux host in your cloud environment or infrastructure for the agent to inspect. IBM Verify: Sign-up for an Identity Provider (IdP) like IBM Verify. Configure OpenID Connect (OIDC) and create a user account. A platform engineer will use this account to authenticate Boundary before the agent opens a session. You can also use other IdPs of your choice. HashiCorp Cloud Platform (HCP) account: Create a free HCP account, deploy Boundary and Vault clusters and complete the following configurations: Configure the Linux host as a Boundary target. Enable session recording for the target and configure an Amazon S3 or supported S3-compatible storage bucket and the applicable storage policies. Store the host credentials in a Boundary static credential store, or, preferably, configure a Vault credential library. Bind the credential source to the SSH target as an injected application credential. Credential injection removes the need for the agent to receive the target credential. Configure Verify as an OIDC authentication provider in Boundary and set the OIDC method as the primary method. Configure Boundary roles and grants to give the authenticated identity least-privilege access to the required target. Local development environment: Install Python and the Boundary CLI on your development machine. The AI agent developed calls watsonx.ai python APIs and connects to the target through a Boundary-proxied session after the platform engineer authenticates. title: [CNCF] Volcano v1.16 Released: NamespaceQueue, fairshare, and a broader HyperNode ecosystem
summary: Volcano v1.16.0 is available . v1.16.0 introduces NamespaceQueue and the fairshare plugin. Tenants can use hierarchical queues within their own namespaces to organize quotas and queue hierarchies within administrator-authorized resource pools. Fairshare brings historical resource consumption into scheduling decisions among namespaces sharing a queue, improving fairness across teams. This release also expands the HyperNode ecosystem. Platforms using other schedulers can deploy the HyperNode controller on its own to discover topology and manage supernodes and their hierarchy, then integrate that information through the HyperNode API. For inference services using Volcano, new PodGroup topology anti-affinity rules can spread instances across supernodes to reduce exposure to a shared failure domain. Scheduler performance improvements include an Unschedulable Job Cache that records why Jobs could not be scheduled and skips repeated checks until blocking conditions change. Node scoring, cache updates, and queue lookups also become more efficient. The release additionally brings Kubernetes 1.36 support, load estimation for bulk Pod dispatch, DRA scoring, and accelerator and stability improvements. Highlights Scheduler Performance and Scalability: An unschedulable Job cache reduces backlog retries, alongside improvements to node scoring, cache updates, and queue lookups. Namespace-local Queue Hierarchies: Tenants can manage hierarchical queues, quotas, and resource sharing within their namespaces and administrator-authorized resource pools. Long-Term Fairness with fairshare: Slurm-inspired usage decay improves fairness for tenants isolated by namespace and sharing a queue. PodGroup Topology Anti-Affinity: Required and preferred rules separate workload instances across HyperNode domains. A Broader HyperNode Ecosystem: Other schedulers can reuse topology discovery and supernode management without running the other Volcano components. Key Features 1. Scheduler performance and scalability v1.16.0 introduces the Unschedulable Job Cache to improve scheduling under large pending backlogs, alongside improvements to node scoring, cache updates, and queue lookups. Unschedulable Job Cache A Job may remain Pending because its queue is full, the cluster lacks suitable resources, or no node satisfies its placement constraints. Repeating the same scheduling checks in every session adds work without changing that outcome. With a large backlog, these retries also compete with newly submitted Jobs that could run. The new UnschedulableJobCache records why a Job could not be scheduled. Plugins provide event hints that identify changes which could make the Job schedulable. Subsequent sessions skip the checks covered by the cached result until a relevant change requests a retry. This reduces redundant work and improves scheduling performance in clusters with persistent unschedulable backlogs. Key capabilities: Selective skipping: Uses rejection causes to skip enqueue checks, whole-Job evaluation, or checks for particular tasks while respecting gang requirements. Event-driven wakeups: A Node label update can wake a Job blocked by node affinity. Resource release or a Queue change can wake Jobs blocked by resources or quota. Storage and DRA events are also supported through plugin hints. Safe fallback: A Job is cached only when every rejecting plugin provides a safe hint. Other Jobs continue through normal per-session evaluation. Preserved scheduling semantics: Cached Jobs remain visible to pending demand, queue accounting, and gang requirements. Normal checks run again before placement after a wakeup. Bounded retries: A watchdog retries cached Jobs after a configurable maximum skip duration, defaulting to five minutes. The in-memory cache is cleared on scheduler restart. The feature is disabled by default. Enable it with the scheduler feature gate: helm upgrade --install volcano volcano-sh/volcano \ --namespace volcano-system --create-namespace --version 1.16.0 \ --set custom.scheduler_feature_gates="UnschedulableJobCache=true" Initial coverage includes the upstream predicates integrated by Volcano, native Resource Fit, proportion, and non-hierarchical capacity. Hierarchical capacity rejections and rejections from plugins without hint providers continue to be evaluated each session. Optional per-Job debug metrics report skips, wakeups, and watchdog expirations. Related: PRs: #5848, #5644 Design and performance results: Unschedulable Job Cache User guide: Enable the Unschedulable Job Cache Contributor: @JesseStutler Multiple scoring plugins can now score nodes in a shared traversal, reducing scoring overhead when several plugins are active. Node updates and queue lookups also avoid unnecessary object copying and traversal. (#5928, #5556, #5506) Volcano will continue to improve performance and scalability. Future work will explore scheduling efficiency, cache and event processing, and status updates, guided by workload benchmarks and production feedback. 2. NamespaceQueue brings queue hierarchies to Namespaces Platforms use different tenancy models. Some assign resource pools to tenants through cluster-scoped Queues. Others use namespaces as the management boundary for teams or projects and want tenants to configure queue quotas and hierarchies within that boundary. NamespaceQueue supports this namespace-based model, aligning queue management with tenant ownership. NamespaceQueue introduces a namespaced resource with the same resource-governance concepts as Queue, including capability, deserved, guarantee, and reclaimable. Administrators authorize a namespace to attach its queue hierarchy to a cluster Queue through spec.allowedNamespaces. Tenants can then manage their own hierarchy within that boundary. This separates resource-pool authorization from day-to-day tenant queue management. Different namespaces can use the same queue names without sharing queue identity. The feature is disabled by default. The Helm switch enables the participating controller, scheduler, and admission components and selects hierarchical capacity when using the chart’s default scheduler configuration: helm upgrade --install volcano volcano-sh/volcano \ --namespace volcano-system --create-namespace --version 1.16.0 \ --set custom.namespace_queue_enable=true Create the namespace and authorized parent Queue, then the tenant queue: apiVersion: v1 kind: Namespace metadata: name: team-a --- apiVersion: scheduling.volcano.sh/v1beta1 kind: Queue metadata: name: research spec: capability: cpu: "100" memory: "200Gi" deserved: cpu: "100" memory: "200Gi" allowedNamespaces: - team-a --- apiVersion: scheduling.volcano.sh/v1beta1 kind: NamespaceQueue metadata: name: training namespace: team-a spec: parent: cluster/research capability: cpu: "40" memory: "80Gi" deserved: cpu: "40" memory: "80Gi" reclaimable: true Grant tenant RBAC permissions for namespacequeues in the tenant’s namespace. After the NamespaceQueue reports Ready=True and Authorized=True, Jobs and PodGroups in team-a can reference it with: spec: queue: namespace/training Bare names still reference cluster Queues. cluster/<name> identifies a cluster Queue parent, while an unprefixed parent name identifies a NamespaceQueue in the same namespace. Initial scheduling support uses hierarchical capacity. Do not enable proportion alongside it. Related: PRs: #5590, #5629 User guide: NamespaceQueue Design: Namespace-scoped Queues Contributor: @gitGurugu 3. fairshare improves long-term tenant fairness Volcano traditionally organizes resource sharing and quota governance around cluster-scoped Queues, which fits deployments that assign a dedicated queue to each tenant. Other platforms use namespaces as the isolation boundary for teams or projects, with multiple tenants submitting into one Queue. These deployments need fairness within that shared queue as well as fairness across queues. Current-allocation snapshots alone do not capture resource consumption over time. If a namespace keeps submitting GPU jobs, each completed job may be replaced by another from the same namespace. A tenant arriving later can wait even though the earlier tenant has already consumed substantial compute time. Inspired by Slurm fair-share scheduling, the new fairshare plugin identifies tenants by namespace and tracks cumulative resource-seconds for each namespace within a queue. Consumption decays exponentially, with a configurable half-life that defaults to four hours. Namespaces with lower historical consumption receive earlier consideration, while old usage gradually loses influence. Fairshare complements DRF’s current-resource fairness. It influences pending-job ordering and can optionally gate enqueue admission. It does not preempt jobs that are already running. Operators can choose target queues and resource types and optionally persist usage state to a ConfigMap across scheduler restarts. Example scheduler configuration: actions: "enqueue, allocate, backfill" tiers: - plugins: - name: priority - name: gang - name: conformance - name: fairshare arguments: fairshare.targetQueues: "gpu-queue" fairshare.resourceKey: "nvidia.com/gpu" fairshare.halfLifeMinutes: "240" fairshare.enableEnqueueGate: "false" fairshare.persistState: "false" - plugins: - name: drf - name: capacity - name: predicates - name: nodeorder Put fairshare before drf so historical usage can influence comparisons before DRF decides them. Keep priority first when PriorityClass should take precedence. State persistence and enqueue gating are disabled by default. Related: Feature PR: #5161 Design: Fair Share Scheduling User guide: Fairshare Plugin Feature contributor: @dmildh-absci 4. PodGroup topology anti-affinity Keeping each workload instance within one topology domain does not ensure that different instances use separate domains. For example, multiple inference replicas can each satisfy their own network locality constraints but still land in the same supernode. A failure in that domain could affect all instances. The group-topology-affinity plugin adds required and preferred PodGroup anti-affinity across HyperNode domains. Rules select peer PodGroups by their labels and can optionally select namespaces. They compose with networkTopology, allowing each group to stay together while different groups use separate domains. Add these entries to the existing scheduler plugin list, retaining its other actions and plugins: - name: group-topology-affinity arguments: weight: 10 - name: network-topology-aware arguments: weight: 10 With a HyperNode tree containing the supernode tier, configure each participating PodGroup as follows, changing the name for each instance: apiVersion: scheduling.volcano.sh/v1beta1 kind: PodGroup metadata: name: inference-a namespace: default labels: app: model-a spec: minMember: 2 queue: default networkTopology: mode: hard highestTierName: supernode topologyAffinity: podGroupAntiAffinity: required: - podGroupSelector: matchLabels: app: model-a topologyTierName: supernode Member Pods must use schedulerName: volcano and the scheduling.k8s.io/group-name annotation. Rules match PodGroup labels, not Pod labels. A term specifies either topologyTierName or topologyTier. Preferred rules additionally use a weight from 1 to 100. Enforcement applies to allocate. BestEffort Pods placed through backfill do not receive this isolation guarantee. SubGroup affinity and anti-affinity, cross-PodGroup affinity, and automatic relocation of running Pods are outside the implemented scope. Related: PR: #5349 Design: PodGroup Topology Affinity User guide: PodGroup Anti-Affinity Contributor: @wangyang0616 5. Expanding the HyperNode ecosystem to more schedulers Platforms using alternative schedulers may also need to discover cluster topology and manage supernodes and their hierarchy. Previously, reusing HyperNode required running Volcano’s aggregate controller manager. v1.16.0 makes the HyperNode controller independently deployable, opening its topology discovery and management capabilities to more scheduling systems. Platforms can deploy just this controller and reuse existing discovery methods, including UFM and node labels. The controller creates and updates HyperNode resources and maintains the supernode hierarchy. Other schedulers can read this information through the HyperNode API and implement topology-aware placement for their workloads, without running the Volcano scheduler or its other controllers. Standalone and integrated deployments share the discovery and reconciliation implementation, allowing future discovery methods to serve both modes. Scheduling systems can share these capabilities and contribute improvements to a common implementation. The release provides a dedicated vc-hypernode-controller-manager binary, image, and Helm Deployment. The chart supports controller-manager, standalone, and disabled modes, with integrated controller-manager mode retained as the default. To install only the HyperNode controller: helm upgrade --install volcano volcano-sh/volcano \ --namespace volcano-system --create-namespace --version 1.16.0 \ --set custom.hypernode_controller_mode=standalone \ --set custom.controller_enable=false \ --set custom.scheduler_enable=false \ --set custom.admission_enable=false Discovery continues to use custom.controller_config_override. To retain the other Volcano components, change only the HyperNode mode. When migrating an existing deployment, first select disabled and wait for the controller-manager rollout before enabling standalone, ensuring a single reconciliation owner. Related: PRs: #5137, #5136 Design: Standalone HyperNode Controller User guide: Install the Standalone HyperNode Controller Discovery configuration: HyperNode Auto Discovery Contributor: @wangyang0616 Other notable enhancements In addition to major features, Volcano 1.16.0 brings several key enhancements: Load-Aware Scheduling for Bulk Pod Dispatch, Queue Resource Limits per Nodegroup, More Accurate NUMA Resource Accounting, DRA and Accelerator Enhancements, HyperNode Discovery and Placement Consistency, Grove and KubeRay Adopt Multi-Level Gang Scheduling, Kubernetes Compatibility and Operations. And the release also delivers essential updates across stability, correctness, and security fixes. For a complete inventory of all improvements and detailed commit histories, please refer to the release note. Upgrade Notes Upgrade to v1.16.0 through Helm or the release manifest: helm repo add volcano-sh https://volcano-sh.github.io/helm-charts helm repo update helm upgrade volcano volcano-sh/volcano \ --namespace volcano-system --version 1.16.0 Update CRDs and RBAC with the components before using NamespaceQueue or the new PodGroup and Numatopology fields. NamespaceQueue and UnschedulableJobCache are disabled by default. NamespaceQueue requires hierarchical capacity, whose rejections are not cached by this cache version. Review fairshare plugin order and topology anti-affinity enforcement scope before enabling them. Rebuild custom topology plugins for HyperNodeGradientResult and review the Kubernetes 1.36 integration changes. Source builds require Go 1.26. When moving HyperNode reconciliation to the standalone controller, roll out disabled mode before standalone. The existing Volcano CRDs receive retention annotations for Helm uninstall. The new NamespaceQueue CRD does not carry that annotation in this version. Review retention and ownership before reinstalling. Acknowledgements Volcano v1.16 was made possible by the collective efforts of 65 dedicated contributors around the world. Sincere thanks to everyone who contributed features, fixes, testing, documentation, and reviews—your ongoing support continues to drive Volcano’s scheduling capabilities and stability forward!
