For the complete API changes, bug fixes, dependency updates, maintenance items, and full list of contributors, please refer to the release notes： Release Note Full Changelog

title: [CNCF] Isolation. Security. Scale.
summary: Without these three things, Agents cannot be properly implemented in a controlled environment, they will not have policy enforcement to ensure they do what they’re supposed to do, and there’s zero way of ensuring that the Agent will be readily available when needed. Kagent as the runtime for declarative and BYO (covering frameworks like langgraph/ADK) Agents combined with Agent Substrate for the underlying sandbox environment ensures that you can implement all three production-level needs when running agentic workloads. In this blog post, you’ll learn the key concepts to agent sandboxing, how Substrate is used, and implementing it with kagent. Prerequisites To follow along with this blog post in a hands-on fashion, you will need: A Kubernetes cluster (local cluster like Kind or Minikube is fine). If you do not have a k8s cluster, you can follow along from a theoretical perspective for the learnings until you have a cluster readily available. Agent sandboxing as a whole If you spin up Docker or whatever containerization engine you prefer, create a container, and run a workload in it, technically speaking the workload is “sandboxed”. However, that level of sandboxing might as well not even exist. Ingress and egress is wide open, the workload can send packets to whatever it likes, and there’s zero policy enforcement. Of course there are ways to tighten this up (network policies, segmentation, routing rules, etc.), but that doesn’t change the fact that sandboxing as a whole is “flat” by nature. Sandboxing an Agent in a secure and effective fashion means: Untrusted agent code cannot escape into the host environment or compromise underlying infrastructure. The blast radius for a harness is minimized. The Agent that holds onto model output, possibility credentials, and tool calls is within an isolated boundary. Agents are snapshotted so it knows where to pick up where it left off (where the state exists). Agent multiplexing (routing traffic to multiple Agents) in a multi-tenant environment is isolated and has a boundary. To ensure that the above can be properly implemented, you need the ability to isolate Agents at both the hardware and software level along with policy enforcement at the AI Gateway for when Agent traffic is reaching its destination. Where does agent substrate fit In? Container isolation (and software-level isolation to that point) stops at your kernel. Everything is running in said kernel (in the user space), which can be sufficient for some, but how that isolation is implemented matters. How the client routes to the Agent and what is in the middle facilitating that routing is what counts when it comes to isolation. That’s where Agent Substrate comes into play. With Agent Substrate, all Agents are running in Workers, which are Pods. The Agents are facilitated via Actors, which are managed by the ateapi (Agent Substrate’s Control Plane). Where the isolation comes into play is with software and hardware-level isolation. gVisor is used for software-level isolation and microVM is used for hardware-level isolation. With software-level isolation, the isolated workload runs inside of the user space using a dedicated user-space app kernel called Sentry that intercepts and handles system calls. MicroVM guest OS/VM runs directly on physical CPU cores using hardware-level virtualization extensions. Running in the user space/namespace (e.g., software level isolation) is a decision for the system, like gVisor. Using substrate in Kagent In the previous sections, you learned about the architecture, design, and system choices for why sandboxing an Agent is important. In the upcoming sections, you’ll learn how to do it in a hands-on fashion with kagent and Agent Substrate. The interaction points you’ll see where is; kagent is the runtime, Agent Substrate is the platform sitting understand to help implement and facilitate sandboxing. Without kagent, the only real entry point to interact with Agent Substrate is via a programmatic call with something like a curl to interact with the Actor. Kagent allows you to interact with Agents running in Actors via Substrate in a way that the industry is comfortable with (a UI and in a declarative fashion). Installation and Configuration There are a few steps to installing kagent v1.0 and Agent Substrate, including: Configuring kubectl-ate (to interact with Agent Substrate via the CLI). The installation of Agent Substrate itself Installing kagent To get a play-by-play, step-by-step instruction set, you can take a look at the guide found here. Once you’re up and running, you’ll see that with the Helm installation of kagent by default, one WorkerPool gets created with two Workers (Pods). The WorkerPool gets created with the substrateWorkerPool.create=true setting on the Helm Chart. Creating an agent programmatically With kagent + Agent Substrate installed, you can now create an Agent (Actor) and an Agent Template. The AgentTemplate is like a “golden image” (although, “image” feels a bit too heavy of wording) that contains the configurations for your Agent and can be reused across Agents that you deploy. The Harness is the Actor (Agent) itself. This can be something like a Harness (Codex, Claude Code, etc.) or a BYO Agent using a framework like langgraph. Run the below to declaratively create the Harness and AgentTemplate using the kagent CRDs. kubectl apply -f - <<EOF apiVersion: kagent.dev/v1alpha3 kind: Harness metadata: name: kagent namespace: kagent spec: kagent: {} workload: image: PATH_TO_YOUR_AGENT_IMAGE substrate: workerPoolRef: name: kagent-default snapshotPolicy: location: gs://ate-snapshots-PATH_TO_YOUR_SNAPSHOTS allowedAgentTemplates: selector: matchLabels: kagent.dev/harness: kagent --- apiVersion: kagent.dev/v1alpha3 kind: AgentTemplate metadata: name: assistant namespace: kagent labels: kagent.dev/harness: kagent spec: modelConfig: name: default-model-config description: A substrate-backed assistant used to verify this main build. systemPrompt: You are a helpful assistant running on kagent. EOF Once deployed, you’ll see the Agent running in kagent along with the template. Creating an agent in the UI Aside from creating an Agent in a declarative fashion, you can also create one in the UI. Within the UI, click on the Agents pane. Click the purple + New template button. You can then define the template like how you did in the YAML within the previous section. Go into the Harness configuration via the purple + New Harness section. Within there is where you can define the harness like you did declaratively in the previous section to point to the Namespace that you want the Actor/Agent deployed in, the name, runtime adapter, and the location where the image exists. Using a sandboxed agent When you open the Agents tab, you’ll see the `assistant` Agent. Then, go over to the Substrate tab. Notice how it says 0/8 Actors running? That’s because an Actor is only running when there’s an active session (this ties back to the efficiency of hardware resources when using Agent Substrate) Next, open your Agent and prompt it with whatever you’d like. You’ll now see that there are 0/9 Actors. The reason why is because when you start a new session, a new Actor spins up. It then spins down once the session is complete (the session being what you’re asking the Agent and when it responds). If you open a new session and prompt the Agent, you’ll see 0/10. If you use an existing session, the Actor count won’t change because it’s still the same session. This is important because it can look like “every time I use an Agent, a new Actor spins up and that’s a lot of resources to manage”, but it’s only when a new session occurs. Wrapping Up In this section, you not only learned about why sandboxing is important and the key projects driving sandboxing forward, but how to deploy Actors within kagent using Agent Substrate as the sandbox platform/architecture. Moving forward for engineering teams and enterprises alike, having the ability to isolate, secure, govern, and control Agents will be key to truly understanding what your Agents can and can’t do, which is a key holding point today for many organizations when implementing Agents.

title: [CNCF] Multi-tenant GPU Kubernetes on simulated hardware with Kamaji and HAMi
summary: GPU teams usually face a bad trade-off. Give every team its own Kubernetes cluster and you pay for a control plane per team. Put everyone in one shared cluster and you get weak isolation. Either way, Kubernetes hands out GPUs as whole cards, so a pod that needs 4 GB of an 80 GB GPU still blocks the entire card. This post shows a way out by combining two open-source projects: Kamaji runs each tenant’s Kubernetes control plane as pods inside one management cluster. HAMi lets pods request a slice of a GPU (memory in MB, compute in %) and packs several pods onto one card. I built the whole thing on a single machine with no physical GPU, using HAMi’s mock device plugin to simulate the cards. The result: two fully isolated tenant clusters, each scheduling fractional-GPU workloads through HAMi, with all eight tests passing. Everything below is reproducible: the exact versions, the commands that worked, the errors I hit and how I fixed them. Architecture One kind cluster hosts Kamaji and both tenant control planes; each tenant’s worker is a separate container that joins over the kind network and runs HAMi. Tenants never share a node or an API server. The only shared pieces are the management cluster and the kamaji-etcd datastore, where each tenant’s data is kept separate. Why Kamaji + HAMi Kamaji solves the cluster problem and HAMi solves the GPU problem; they work at different layers, so they don’t overlap. The interesting part is where they meet. A tenant’s API server lives in the management cluster, but HAMi’s webhook lives on the tenant’s worker nodes. Every GPU pod creation therefore depends on the API server reaching back into the tenant through Kamaji’s Konnectivity tunnel. Proving that path works was the main goal of this lab. Lab setup Everything runs as Docker containers on one Linux host; 4 CPU cores, 8 GB of free RAM and 20 GB of disk are enough. How do you test GPU sharing without a GPU? HAMi’s real device plugin talks to the NVIDIA driver, so it can’t start without hardware. The mock device plugin skips hardware discovery. You describe fake cards in a node annotation, and it registers gpumem and gpucores capacity from that. HAMi’s webhook, scheduler and quota logic then run exactly as they would on real nodes. Two simulated setups make the tenants easy to tell apart: tenant-a: 1 × NVIDIA A100 80 GB (81,920 MB, 100 cores) tenant-b: 2 × NVIDIA L4 24 GB (49,152 MB, 200 cores) Step-by-step build The build has five steps; step 3 creates both tenants at once, and steps 4 and 5 are repeated per tenant. Plain kubectl talks to the management cluster; --kubeconfig tenant-a.kubeconfig talks to a tenant. Step 1: Management cluster, cert-manager and MetalLB kind create cluster --name kamaji kubectl apply -f https://github.com/cert-manager/cert-manager/releases/download/v1.21.2/cert-manager.yaml kubectl -n cert-manager wait pod --all --for=condition=Ready --timeout=180s kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/metallb/metallb/v0.16.1/config/manifests/metallb-frr-k8s.yaml kubectl -n metallb-system wait pod --all --for=condition=Ready --timeout=180s Find your kind network’s IPv4 subnet, then give MetalLB a range at the top of it: docker network inspect kind | grep Subnet cat <<EOF | kubectl apply -f - apiVersion: metallb.io/v1beta1 kind: IPAddressPool metadata: name: kind-ip-pool namespace: metallb-system spec: addresses: - 172.18.255.200-172.18.255.250 --- apiVersion: metallb.io/v1beta1 kind: L2Advertisement metadata: name: empty namespace: metallb-system EOF Step 2: Install Kamaji helm repo add clastix https://clastix.github.io/charts helm upgrade --install kamaji clastix/kamaji \ --namespace kamaji-system --create-namespace \ --set 'resources=null' --version 0.0.0+latest kubectl -n kamaji-system get pods Step 3: Create the Tenant Control Planes This creates both tenants, tenant-a and tenant-b: export TENANT_VERSION=v1.36.4 kubectl create namespace tenants for t in tenant-a tenant-b; do cat <<EOF | kubectl apply -f - apiVersion: kamaji.clastix.io/v1alpha1 kind: TenantControlPlane metadata: name: ${t} namespace: tenants labels: tenant.clastix.io: ${t} spec: controlPlane: deployment: replicas: 1 service: serviceType: LoadBalancer kubernetes: version: "${TENANT_VERSION}" kubelet: configurationJSONPatches: - op: add path: /cgroupDriver value: systemd networkProfile: port: 6443 podCidr: 10.244.0.0/16 addons: coreDNS: {} kubeProxy: {} konnectivity: server: port: 8132 agent: mode: DaemonSet EOF done Once both tenant control plane pods are Running, save a kubeconfig for each tenant: for t in tenant-a tenant-b; do kubectl -n tenants get secret ${t}-admin-kubeconfig -o jsonpath='{.data.admin\.conf}' | base64 -d > ${t}.kubeconfig kubectl --kubeconfig ${t}.kubeconfig cluster-info Done Each tenant control plane is a single pod in the tenants namespace of the management cluster, running on the kamaji-control-plane node. The 4/4 in the READY column are its four containers: kube-apiserver: the tenant’s API server, exposed through the MetalLB IP kube-scheduler: the tenant’s default scheduler kube-controller-manager: runs the tenant’s built-in controllers konnectivity-server: the management-cluster end of the tunnel that lets the API server reach the tenant’s worker nodes Step 4: Join a worker node Kamaji has no kind helper for workers, so the worker is a kindest/node container on the kind network, joined with standard kubeadm. Its version must match the tenant. docker run -d --name tenant-a-worker --hostname tenant-a-worker \ --network kind --privileged \ --security-opt seccomp=unconfined --security-opt apparmor=unconfined \ --tmpfs /tmp --tmpfs /run -v /var -v /lib/modules:/lib/modules:ro \ kindest/node:v1.36.4@sha256:099e049362a1526b2db71494e1947aae99bd16290d7c895f2b7ea312e3cbfaed sleep 15 docker exec -i tenant-a-worker sh -c 'cat > /root/tenant-a.kubeconfig' < tenant-a.kubeconfig JOIN_CMD=$(docker exec tenant-a-worker kubeadm token create --print-join-command \ --kubeconfig /root/tenant-a.kubeconfig) echo "$JOIN_CMD" docker exec tenant-a-worker bash -c "${JOIN_CMD} --ignore-preflight-errors=all" Install Calico in the tenant (not the management cluster), with its pool set to the tenant podCidr: curl -sLO https://raw.githubusercontent.com/projectcalico/calico/v3.31.2/manifests/calico.yaml sed -i 's|# - name: CALICO_IPV4POOL_CIDR|- name: CALICO_IPV4POOL_CIDR|; s|# value: "192.168.0.0/16"| value: "10.244.0.0/16"|' calico.yaml kubectl --kubeconfig tenant-a.kubeconfig apply -f calico.yaml kubectl --kubeconfig tenant-a.kubeconfig get nodes Step 5: HAMi and mock GPUs in the tenant # Don’t label the worker gpu=on; that starts HAMi’s real NVIDIA device plugin, which fails without a driver. export KUBECONFIG=$PWD/tenant-a.kubeconfig helm repo add hami-charts https://project-hami.github.io/HAMi/ helm install hami hami-charts/hami -n kube-system # wait for hami-scheduler Running, and the hami-scheduler-device ConfigMap to exist kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Project-HAMi/mock-device-plugin/master/k8s-mock-rbac.yaml kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Project-HAMi/mock-device-plugin/master/k8s-mock-plugin.yaml # Simulate 1 x A100 80 GB NODE=tenant-a-worker kubectl patch node $NODE --subresource=status --type=json \ -p '' kubectl annotate node $NODE \ 'hami.io/node-nvidia-register=' About 30 seconds later the node advertises the fake card: { "nvidia.com/gpu": "10", "nvidia.com/gpucores": "100", "nvidia.com/gpumem": "81920", "nvidia.com/gpumem-percentage": "100" } For tenant-b, repeat steps 4 and 5 with tenant-b names. Its annotation describes two cards (GPU-MOCK-B0 and GPU-MOCK-B1, 24,576 MB and 100 cores each), with nvidia.com/gpu capacity set to 20. How a GPU pod gets scheduled A GPU pod crosses from the management cluster into the tenant and back before it lands on a node, and that round trip is what makes the two projects work together. The dashed hop is the key integration point. The API server runs inside the management cluster, but HAMi’s webhook runs on the tenant worker, so the admission call travels through Kamaji’s Konnectivity tunnel. If that hop failed, GPU pods would fall back to the default scheduler and HAMi would never see them. Test results All eight tests passed. TC-03 and TC-05: three pods share one card Each pod asks for 20,000 MB and 30% of a GPU. This loop creates all three. After each pod is scheduled, it releases HAMi’s node lock by hand, because the mock plugin never does (see gotcha 2): export KUBECONFIG=$PWD/tenant-a.kubeconfig for i in 1 2 3; do cat <<EOF | kubectl apply -f - apiVersion: v1 kind: Pod metadata: name: gpu-share-${i} spec: containers: - name: app image: busybox command:  resources: limits: nvidia.com/gpu: 1 nvidia.com/gpumem: 20000 # MB nvidia.com/gpucores: 30 # % of one card EOF kubectl wait pod/gpu-share-${i} --for=condition=PodScheduled --timeout=120s kubectl annotate pod gpu-share-${i} hami.io/bind-phase=success --overwrite kubectl annotate node tenant-a-worker hami.io/mutex.lock- done The webhook routed the pod to HAMi, and HAMi placed it on the mock card: $ kubectl get pod gpu-share-1 -o jsonpath='{.spec.schedulerName}' Hami-scheduler Annotations: hami.io/vgpu-devices-allocated: GPU-MOCK-0,NVIDIA,20000,30:; hami.io/vgpu-node: tenant-a-worker Events: Normal FilteringSucceed hami-scheduler find fit node(tenant-a-worker), 0 nodes not fit, 1 nodes fit Normal BindingSucceed hami-scheduler Successfully binding node  to default/gpu-share-1 Three such pods ended up running on the same card: 60,000 MB and 90% of compute in use. NAME READY STATUS NODE gpu-share-1 1/1 Running tenant-a-worker gpu-share-2 1/1 Running tenant-a-worker gpu-share-3 1/1 Running tenant-a-worker TC-06 and TC-07: HAMi refuses to over-commit A fourth 30% pod would need 120 of 100 cores: cat <<EOF | kubectl apply -f - apiVersion: v1 kind: Pod metadata: name: gpu-share-4 spec: containers: - name: app image: busybox command:  resources: limits: nvidia.com/gpu: 1 nvidia.com/gpumem: 20000 # MB nvidia.com/gpucores: 30 # % of one card EOF It stays Pending, and HAMi names the reason: $ kubectl describe pod gpu-share-4 | sed -n '/Events/,$p' Events: Type Reason Age From Message ---- ------ ---- ---- ------- Warning FailedScheduling 15s hami-scheduler 0/1 nodes are available: 1 1/1 CardInsufficientCore. no new claims to deallocate, preemption: 0/1 nodes are available: 1 No preemption victims found for incoming pod. Warning FilteringFailed 15s (x2 over 15s) hami-scheduler 1 nodes CardInsufficientCore(tenant-a-worker) Warning FilteringFailed 15s (x2 over 15s) hami-scheduler no available node, 1 nodes do not meet A pod asking for 90,000 MB exceeds the 81,920 MB card: cat <<EOF | kubectl apply -f - apiVersion: v1 kind: Pod metadata: name: gpu-mem-big spec: containers: - name: app image: busybox command:  resources: limits: nvidia.com/gpu: 1 nvidia.com/gpumem: 90000 # MB, more than the whole card nvidia.com/gpucores: 10 # % of one card, fits in the free 10% EOF It stays Pending, this time with CardInsufficientMemory. TC-08: tenants can’t see each other Run the same queries against each tenant’s API server and compare what comes back: for t in a b; do echo "===== tenant-$t =====" kubectl --kubeconfig tenant-$t.kubeconfig get nodes kubectl --kubeconfig tenant-$t.kubeconfig get pods -A | grep -E 'gpu-|NAME' kubectl --kubeconfig tenant-$t.kubeconfig get nodes -o json \ | jq '.items.status.allocatable | with_entries(select(.key|test("gpumem|gpucores")))' done ===== tenant-a ===== NAME STATUS ROLES AGE VERSION tenant-a-worker Ready <none> 29m v1.36.4 NAMESPACE NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE default gpu-share-1 1/1 Running 0 14m default gpu-share-2 1/1 Running 0 12m default gpu-share-3 1/1 Running 0 12m { "nvidia.com/gpucores": "100", "nvidia.com/gpumem": "81920", "nvidia.com/gpumem-percentage": "100" } ===== tenant-b ===== NAME STATUS ROLES AGE VERSION tenant-b-worker Ready <none> 5m28s v1.36.4 NAMESPACE NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE { "nvidia.com/gpucores": "200", "nvidia.com/gpumem": "49152", "nvidia.com/gpumem-percentage": "200" } Each tenant sees only its own worker, its own pods and its own GPU capacity: Both control planes run in the same management cluster, yet neither tenant’s API returns anything belonging to the other. Gotchas and fixes Few things broke along the way; each has a one-line fix. 1. IPv6 on the kind network broke the MetalLB pool. The gateway lookup from the Kamaji guide printed fc00:f853:ccd:e793::1172.18.0.1, with the IPv6 and IPv4 gateways glued together. Fix: read the IPv4 subnet with docker network inspect kind | grep Subnet and write the range (172.18.255.200-172.18.255.250) directly. 2. GPU pods stuck on “node lock contention”. After the first GPU pod, the next ones stayed Pending with: Warning BindingFailed hami-scheduler node tenant-a-worker has been locked within 5m0s: node lock contention HAMi locks a node while binding a pod and marks it hami.io/bind-phase: allocating. On real nodes, HAMi’s device plugin completes the allocation and releases the lock. The mock plugin doesn’t, so the lock only expires after 5 minutes. Fix for the lab: do the device plugin’s job by hand. kubectl annotate pod gpu-share-1 hami.io/bind-phase=success --overwrite kubectl annotate node tenant-a-worker hami.io/mutex.lock- The next pod bound within seconds. This is a mock-only artifact, not a Kamaji or HAMi bug. What this lab does not prove The lab proves the wiring and the scheduling decisions, not runtime GPU isolation. No real memory or compute limits. HAMi-core enforces GPU limits inside the container through the NVIDIA driver. A mock card has nothing to enforce. No performance data. No CUDA workloads ran, so throughput and noisy-neighbour effects are untested. Hand-made device data. On real nodes, HAMi’s device plugin writes the node annotation and completes each allocation; here I did both by hand. Unofficial worker path. Joining kindest/node containers works, but Kamaji’s supported route for workers is kubeadm on real machines or Cluster API. Conclusion Kamaji and HAMi fit together without any glue code. Kamaji gives each team its own Kubernetes API without a control plane machine per team, and HAMi turns each GPU into a pool of slices inside those clusters. The one real integration risk, the hosted API server calling HAMi’s webhook back through Konnectivity, worked on the first try. If you have no GPU, the mock device plugin is enough to build and test the whole platform before you buy one.

title: [Cloudflare] Cloudflare DDoS Threat Report 2026 Q3: More swarms, fewer giants
summary: Welcome to the 26th edition of Cloudflare's DDoS Threat Report. This edition covers the third quarter of 2026 — July, August, and September — and returns the series to its quarterly cadence following the combined H1 2026 volume. The analysis is produced by Cloudforce One, Cloudflare's Threat Intelligence organization, providing a comprehensive analysis of the evolving threat landscape of Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attacks based on data from the Cloudflare network.Key insightsShort-burst, low-bandwidth attacks lasting under 10 minutes and 1 Gbps surged by 208%. Conversely, hyper-volumetric attacks exceeding 1 Tbps plummeted by nearly 69% from Q2, possibly a reflection of law enforcement actions against four major Internet of Things (IoT) botnets earlier in the year. However, variants continue to emerge, proving that IoT botnets remain a durable, high-volume threat to network infrastructure.Threat actors dramatically shifted their reflection and amplification tactics, abruptly abandoning CLDAP floods, which collapsed by 99.5% quarter-over-quarter. Instead, attackers pivoted heavily toward other connectionless protocols, driving a 215% surge in DNS amplification and a 122% increase in general UDP floods.Attack targets broadened significantly across both industries and geographies, with the United States reclaiming the most-attacked position from China. Canada and Israel experienced sharp spikes in targeted attacks — jumping 10 and 7 spots respectively — while juggling geopolitical tensions, trade disputes, and contentious domestic events. At the same time, the operational focus shifted away from media organizations toward a wider array of industry targets, including consumer services, Internet infrastructure, and adult entertainment.Q3 by the numbers: 8,200 DDoS attacks every hourAcross its network in the third quarter of 2026, Cloudflare autonomously mitigated 18.2 million network-layer DDoS attacks and 14.4 trillion HTTP DDoS requests. That works out to approximately 8,226 network-layer DDoS attacks per hour, or about 197,400 per day — one attack every 0.44 seconds. The quarter's mitigated traffic totaled 272.6 PB at the network layer and 95.1 PB at the HTTP layer.More swarms, fewer giantsShort-burst, mid-range, high-count attacks — the operational signature of DDoS-for-hire "booter" services — accelerated this quarter. These attacks primarily targeted computer software, gambling and casinos, and information technology industries. Cloudflare autonomously mitigated 18.2 million network-layer DDoS attacks in Q3 2026, a +208% increase from the same quarter in 2025:96% ended in under 10 minutes98% stayed under 1 Gbps, more than enough to overwhelm a server or websiteOn the other hand, network-level hyper-volumetric attacks (those exceeding 1 Tbps) reversed course, dropping to 251 attacks in Q3 from 805 in Q2 — coinciding with law enforcement action in early 2026 that dismantled four of the largest IoT DDoS botnets: Aisuru, KimWolf, JackSkid, and Mossad.Still, IoT-based botnets remain a durable high-volume threat as the ecosystem churns through new variants such as Dysphoria and Evooo1Bot. Mirai-classified mitigation peaked in August at 57.23 PB, representing 46.5% of all mitigated network-layer bytes in Q3, including four days — August 16, 19, 23, and 25 — that each cleared three petabytes. The quarter's longest sustained Mirai attack ran 49.7 hours between August 19 and August 21.Vector shifts: the collapse of CLDAP and rise of UDPThe most dramatic vector shift of the quarter was downward. CLDAP (Connectionless Lightweight Directory Access Protocol) attacks — where small queries with a forged victim IP address trick public domain controllers (UDP 389) into reflecting massive, amplified responses back at the target — experienced a dramatic +580% quarter-over-quarter surge in the first half of the year before collapsing to just 0.05% of attacks in Q3.Meanwhile, DNS amplification surged 215% to account for 3.43% of all network-layer attacks, exploiting open DNS resolvers in a similar reflection-and-amplification pattern to CLDAP: small spoofed queries, large replies directed at the victim. Other UDP floods climbed from 14.06% to 31.31% of network-layer attacks. UDP is a connectionless transport protocol, which makes it a convenient vehicle for raw volumetric attacks: attackers send large numbers of UDP packets to random or specific ports on the target, forcing the target to check for a listening application and respond, consuming its network and compute resources.Most-attacked industryWhile Media, Production & Publishing remained the most-attacked industry in Q3 2026, its overall share is roughly a quarter of its Q2 level, and the focus has moved across a wider set of industries. Internet rose from outside the top 10 to #6; Consumer Services and Adult Entertainment also climbed in, reaching #8 and #9 respectively.Most-attacked locationsGeographic surges: Canada and Israel climb the ranksAdding to an already turbulent period of bilateral trade disputes, Canada jumped from #16 to #6, driven by attacks against its Retail, Telecommunications, Service providers & carriers, and Marketing & advertising industries.Israel moved 7 spots to take #10 as a result of sustained DDoS activity in mid-September. While this period was marked by contentious decisions ahead of parliamentary elections and the Rosh Hashanah holiday, there was also a massive, documented surge in hostile cyber warfare targeting Israel this year.Top 10The United States was the most-attacked location in Q3 2026, while China was number #2 and Indonesia rose into the top three at 2.93% of total attacks. The U.S.-China pairing at the top is consistent with the first half of 2026, when China finished #1 and the U.S. #2; the countries have traded positions as attention and attacker preferences shift.Strengthening global defenses and helping to defend the InternetCloudflare's network is designed to absorb this kind of growth in DDoS threats. Every service on our network is protected by free, unmetered DDoS protection that runs at every one of our 330+ cities globally, backed by 500 Tbps of network capacity. Autonomy is the point: our systems detect and mitigate attacks without human intervention. And they need to, because as this quarter's distributions make clear, most attacks end long before a human analyst could see the alert, and the largest attacks still regularly exceed 1 Tbps at a cadence measured in hundreds per quarter.To help hosting providers, cloud computing platforms, and Internet service providers identify and take down the abusive IP addresses and accounts that launch these attacks, we leverage Cloudflare's unique vantage point on DDoS attacks to provide a free DDoS Botnet Threat Feed for Service Providers.Over 800 networks worldwide have signed up for this feed, and we've already seen great collaboration across the community to take down botnet nodes. For a continuously-updated view of attack trends across the Internet, visit Cloudflare Radar.About Cloudforce OneDriven by a mission to help defend the Internet, Cloudforce One draws on telemetry from Cloudflare's global network — which protects more than 20% of the web — to drive threat research and operational response, protecting critical systems for millions of organizations worldwide.

title: [Dropbox Tech] Evolving our calendar assistant Reclaim to be AI-native without starting over
summary: Calendars hold more than just blocks of time. They reflect how people plan their days, coordinate with others, and make room for what matters to them. Reclaim, the Dropbox-owned calendar assistant, helps manage that complexity by using AI to find and adjust time for tasks, habits, and meetings. That approach works well when inputs and expected outcomes are clear. But people also use Reclaim for scheduling that’s less straightforward. As AI assistants and natural-language interfaces became more capable, they opened up a new way for people to use Reclaim. We imagined situations where users could describe a scheduling goal in their own words, even when it didn’t map neatly to an existing setting or command. Words alone wouldn’t be enough to determine what should happen on a real calendar, though. Reclaim still needs the context that gives requests meaning, including what’s already scheduled, when a user is available, and which preferences and commitments impact changes. Connecting natural-language requests with the surrounding calendar context could help people spend less time figuring out which settings or actions to use. But building the experience required more than adding an AI interface to the existing product. We needed to rethink how Reclaim turned conversational requests into calendar changes while preserving the scheduling system already in place. Evolving Reclaim for AI without starting over For our engineers, the rebuild started with the way Reclaim already managed calendars. Calendar changes carry real weight because time is precious and scheduled events often involve other people. Any new AI capability needed to feel like a natural extension of Reclaim, and it needed to work with the scheduling logic already in place. Before the redesign, Reclaim handled calendar changes in two primary ways. Users could make specific changes themselves, like moving an event or updating a setting. And Reclaim’s automated scheduler also worked in the background. It considered each person’s preferences and availability when finding time for tasks, focus work, and recurring routines like lunch, then adjusted those calendar blocks as schedules changed. The emergence of AI agents introduced a potential third way for users to use Reclaim. Instead of choosing a specific setting or command, a user might prefer to describe what they want to do in their own words. An agent could then interpret that request, look at the relevant parts of their calendar, and work out how Reclaim could help. But we needed to address several challenges before introducing agents to the experience. Large language models can interpret the same request in different ways because they generate answers based on patterns in their training data. For example, an open-ended request like “make time for this tomorrow” could lead an agent to find an open block, create a new event, or move something already on the calendar. Each option would affect the user’s schedule differently, and some could affect other people’s calendars, too. That variability made AI agents different from the two paths Reclaim already supported. Although they arrive at decisions differently, all three actors needed to rely on the same scheduling logic. Creating a separate AI-only path would have duplicated functionality and made Reclaim’s behavior harder to keep consistent across interfaces. We needed a system that could connect a model to both the right calendar information and Reclaim capabilities while also controlling how it used them. The result was an agent platform designed to work within Reclaim’s existing architecture. Building the agent platform Our agent platform gives a model relevant calendar details and access to Reclaim’s features while controlling what the model can see and do. The model interprets what the user says and figures out what they want. The agent, meanwhile, manages the larger process by providing Reclaim’s instructions, relevant calendar context, and tools (which let it ask Reclaim to look up information or request a specific action). When a tool returns information, the agent can send it back to the model to inform the next step. This repeated exchange is called the agent loop. As part of this process, Reclaim gives the agent the calendar information and tools relevant to each request, rather than access to everything at once. This helps the agent focus on the immediate task and limits it to the appropriate actions. For a more complex request, the agent can give one specific part to a specialized subagent. Internal checklists and review steps help keep the overall request on track. Ultimately, we opted to build the agent loop, tools, and the system for gathering context ourselves, and we connect directly to model providers instead of relying on a broad agent framework. That’s because a framework we initially explored lagged behind the provider APIs we wanted to use and included more structure than Reclaim needed. Owning these parts lets us design them around Reclaim’s scheduling needs, adopt new provider capabilities more quickly, and work with different model providers without rebuilding the rest of the platform. That leaves us with more code to maintain, though using agents to help with that code offsets some of the additional work. The same tool system supports Model Context Protocol (MCP) in two ways. Inside Reclaim’s agent loop, an MCP client lets the agent use compatible tools from other services. Separately, Reclaim’s MCP server makes selected Reclaim tools available through supported AI clients, including Claude and ChatGPT. Those clients use their own models and agent loops, but can call the same tools used within Reclaim. Our agent platform helped Reclaim work through open-ended requests, but we still needed safeguards around any changes it proposed. Users needed a way to review those changes before they reached their actual calendars. Making calendar changes consistent and reviewable Behind the scenes, Reclaim represents each scheduling capability as a Schedule Action, our internal term for a standard operation like creating or updating an event, changing an RSVP, or finding availability. Whether a request comes from a user, the automated scheduler, or an agent, the same Schedule Action type is used, including the same validation and commit process. That shared path matters because a calendar change can affect more than one event. Moving a meeting might change someone’s availability or cause Reclaim to adjust flexible events elsewhere on a user’s calendar. If each actor used a separate implementation, engineers would have to reproduce those rules and keep every version aligned as Reclaim evolved, which would have become tedious over time. Because all three actors use the same Schedule Action, engineers can change how an operation works in one place rather than updating three separate versions. This helps Reclaim behave consistently across its interfaces. But even when Reclaim handles a change consistently, users still need to see whether its wider effects match what they want to do. That’s why we developed Preview Mode, which gives users a temporary version of their calendar where they can review AI suggestions and changes requested through chat before applying them to their actual calendar. Essentially, they’re able to see how an event or settings change would affect the rest of their schedule before it goes live. They can then confirm that the change behaves as expected and review any effects on shared events before calendar updates are sent to other attendees. To keep Preview Mode fast, we reworked the automated scheduler as a pure function, meaning, in part, that it can calculate a proposed schedule without saving anything to the user’s actual calendar. Reclaim can repeat that calculation whenever the user adjusts the preview. Because busy calendars and meetings with several attendees require a lot of data, Reclaim keeps a readily accessible copy in Redis, a data store designed for fast retrieval. It also updates attendee availability within the preview whenever an event moves, so the next calculation reflects the schedule being proposed. Keeping AI workflows connected Reclaim now has a consistent path from a natural-language request to a reviewed calendar change. The agent platform connects models with relevant calendar information and Reclaim features, Schedule Actions route proposed updates through the product’s scheduling logic, and Preview Mode makes their effects visible before anything reaches the calendar or other attendees. Together, these pieces extend Reclaim with AI while preserving the scheduling experience people already rely on. This work also reinforced what AI needs in order to be useful inside an active workflow. A model needs the surrounding information to understand a request, a controlled way to act on it, and a review step before the result moves forward. In Reclaim, a scheduling goal can move from conversation to a proposed schedule and then to an approved calendar update without requiring the user to translate it into a specific setting or command. The long-term value of this rebuild is the freedom to evolve without fragmenting the product. As AI changes how people ask for help, Reclaim can introduce new capabilities through the same scheduling foundation rather than adding a separate experience each time. For Reclaim, this offers a practical framework for expanding AI-assisted workflows as models improve and people find new ways to manage their time. ~ ~ ~ If building innovative products, experiences, and infrastructure excites you, come build the future with us! title: [Dropbox Tech] Dropbox CTO Ali Dasdan on moving from AI adoption to transformation
summary: As AI becomes a starting point for more kinds of work, its usefulness depends on access to an organization’s trusted knowledge and context, including the files, research, feedback, decisions, and project history that give the work meaning. Dropbox helps people bring that context into the supported AI tools they choose while preserving the permissions and controls they expect, so they can spend less time finding, uploading, and re-explaining what already exists. When AI helps them create something new, Dropbox gives that work a trusted, durable home where it can be saved, shared, reviewed, approved, and built on over time. That focus on connected workflows also shapes how we use AI within Dropbox. Access to increasingly capable models can help teams produce more. But turning that output into sustained gains in productivity, quality, and customer impact requires examining workflows from end to end. That includes addressing new bottlenecks as output grows, adapting the platform that supports development, aligning organization-wide incentives, and measuring whether greater speed and volume lead to better outcomes. AI also increases the importance of human judgment. People still need to choose the right problems, give agents the context they need, evaluate the validity of their output, and remain in control of important decisions and actions. Problem solving, communication, and leadership become critical to turning AI-enabled output into real value. Dropbox Chief Technology Officer Ali Dasdan and Senior Director of Engineering Productivity Uma Namasivayam discuss lessons from deploying AI at company scale, how we assess productivity and ROI, how our progress compares with industry peers, and what organizations need to consider as they move from AI adoption to broader transformation. What have you learned in the last year about driving productivity with AI, not just for engineers but across the wider Dropbox organization? Ali: You have to start with the outcome you’re trying to achieve. Giving people AI tools is only the first step. As people use them, your assumptions get tested and new bottlenecks emerge. Maybe you’re coding faster, but now you have too many code reviews. Or you’re generating significantly more code, which puts additional stress on the tools and infrastructure that support development. If you want AI to have a meaningful impact, you have to look at the workflow end to end and keep adapting it until you’re producing the outcome you actually want. There’s no silver bullet. Uma: You have to approach it with a product mindset. Leadership saying, “You need to start using AI tools,” is good, but that alone won’t drive adoption. You also need ground-up awareness through initiatives like boot camps and show-and-tells that involve people more deeply. And you have to align incentives so managers understand what ROI they’re getting from it. How should companies think about measuring AI productivity and ROI? Ali: If I write 10 lines of code and push them to production, it’s almost impossible to prove those 10 lines were responsible for a certain amount of customer satisfaction or revenue improvement. I might produce a million lines a day, but if it’s the wrong product and customers have no interest in it, then it’s not going to work. The real ROI metrics are outcomes like revenue, cost, customer satisfaction, and retention. Then we look at proxy metrics that connect our output to those outcomes. Are we moving faster, producing more code, running more experiments, and pushing more features? Is the site faster and more reliable? There’s no single metric. The framework we use focuses on speed, effectiveness, quality, and impact, with multiple metrics under each. The industry hasn’t found the full solution yet. How does Dropbox’s AI-driven engineering productivity compare with companies operating at a similar level of technical scale and complexity? Ali: If we define peers as top technology companies we hire from and compete with for talent, we’re seeing very similar problems and metrics. We’re around 70% AI-generated code, and Uber recently shared a number around 70%. They see a need for internal agentic coding solutions, and so do we. They have their own tools, and we have Nova, our internal service for running coding agents. Larger companies have allocated more resources to these problems, while we’re super lean. Despite that, I feel like we’re comparable with that peer group across multiple metrics, including how quickly we adopted AI and reached our targets. Compared with the broader industry, it appears we’re ahead. Uma: The industry looks at pull request throughput, or the rate at which teams complete code changes, as one proxy metric for productivity. It’s not ‌perfect, but our throughput ranks in the top 5% in a custom benchmark of companies with similarly large, complex codebases and engineering systems. We also look at whether moving faster affects quality. Our change failure percentage, which measures how often a deployment leads to degraded performance or failure, is in line with industry peers at the 75th percentile. Our token usage is also among the lowest in that peer group, which could indicate that our teams or systems are operating efficiently. Together, these measures give us a fuller picture of how we’re doing against similar companies. As AI usage grows, how do you decide where additional investment is worthwhile? Ali: AI requires money, and when we talk about AI funding, we’re talking about a large portfolio. There are products used by individual functions, capabilities in tools like Zoom and Slack, company-wide deployments like ChatGPT Enterprise, automation tools, and coding models. We’re seeing benefits. People are fixing tech debt, long-running migration projects are getting finished, and we’re delivering most of the roadmap with fewer resources. But organizations still have to decide which ideas to pursue and when to invest more, often before they can draw a direct line to ROI. That requires domain expertise, the right incentives, and a lot of judgment. We’re still working through it along with the rest of the industry. How should companies determine whether their AI spend is creating real value? Ali: At Dropbox, we’re starting to think less about raw token consumption and more about the engineering value those tokens create. With Nova, for example, we can connect agent usage to actual engineering workflows, validation, and outcomes. That gives us a way to evaluate AI spend based on the engineering work those tokens help produce, rather than simply how many tokens we’re consuming. As AI lowers the cost and effort required to produce software, which human skills become more valuable? Ali: If you look fundamentally at what engineers or computer scientists do, it’s that we know how to solve a problem. That’ll never disappear. AI may help me solve bigger problems or solve them faster, but I still need to provide better context, ask the right questions, judge the validity of the answers, know how to iterate, and give a good spec and problem definition. I also need to understand how a solution fits into the broader system and adapt as the tools change. Problem solving, communication, systems thinking, and judgment become even more important because agents depend on people to guide and evaluate their work. Uma: I would give you three things. One is problem solving, which Ali explained really well. The second is judgment. The next phase of AI could make the cost of engineering almost zero, which makes choosing the right problems and evaluating what AI produces extremely important. The third is leadership. Leaders need to understand people, navigate ambiguity as work changes, bring teams together, communicate clearly, build trust, and make sure incentives are aligned. Those skills won’t go away at all. Their value will only grow. As AI models and agents become more widely available, what’ll distinguish the organizations that use them effectively, and what role can Dropbox play? Ali: Models and agents can be incredibly capable, but they don’t automatically know which information an organization trusts, what decisions have already been made, who has access, or what needs to happen next. Without that context, even a strong model can produce generic or incomplete results. Dropbox can connect supported AI experiences to customer-owned content and context, then give the work AI produces a place to be saved, shared, reviewed, approved, and continued. People still make consequential decisions, while the work keeps moving without losing the sources, history, and collaborators behind it. A year from now, what do you hope AI-enabled work looks like at Dropbox? Uma: This year, we’ve focused heavily on engineering, and we’re now starting to understand the workflows across product, design, and other non-engineering teams. A year from now, the goal is for people across those teams to be able to come up with ideas, test them with customers, and potentially ship some of those features. If our customer experience team sees an issue, for example, they could use agents to develop a solution and see whether it works for the customer. That’s the vision we’re pursuing internally. If we can prove it works, we could potentially enable external customers to build on Dropbox platforms and use AI with the building blocks we have. ~ ~ ~ If building innovative products, experiences, and infrastructure excites you, come build the future with us! title: [Microsoft Azure] Managing open-weight model risk in enterprise deployments
summary: The growing AI landscape is giving enterprises more choice in how they build, customize, and deploy increasingly capable models. Open-weight models are an important part of that landscape. They give enterprises access to model weights and greater flexibility to inspect, evaluate, modify, and run models within their own environments. While that flexibility can be valuable, it also affects how enterprises evaluate models, where they implement safeguards, and who is responsible for maintaining those safeguards over time. As enterprises choose which models to deploy, the relevant question is broader than whether a model is open-weight or closed-weight. Enterprises need to understand what they are using the model for, what could go wrong in that context, and what evidence and controls they need to manage risks. Today, Microsoft and NVIDIA are publishing Risk Management for Open-Weight Models in Enterprise, the first in a planned series of joint resources intended to help enterprises address those questions. The paper introduces a shared risk taxonomy and an approach to managing model risks grounded in established standards and frameworks, including International Organization for Standardization (ISO) standards and the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) AI Risk Management Framework. The paper reflects a core idea: weight openness alone does not determine an AI system’s risk. Risk depends on the model, use case, deployment, and safeguards. Read the whitepaper: Risk Management for Open-Weight Models in EnterpriseUnderstanding risk in the deployment contextOpen- and closed-weight models can share many of the same underlying risks, but how those risks materialize depends on the deployment. A model used to help an employee draft a document presents different considerations than the same model used in a customer-facing workflow, just as a standalone inference endpoint differs from a system connected to external data or tools. The architecture matters too. A risk may originate in the model, while the most effective control may sit in the inference environment, application, or surrounding operational processes. The joint guidance looks beyond the model label to factors including provenance, intended use, users, deployment conditions, and surrounding controls. This first paper focuses primarily on model-layer risks. Evaluating a model alone does not establish the safety of an agent or application: teams must also assess its permissions, data access, tools, runtime, and operational controls. Establishing a common languageManaging these risks consistently also requires a common vocabulary across engineering, security, legal, safety, and business teams. The initial Microsoft and NVIDIA taxonomy organizes risks into five broad categories: Cybersecurity, Data Protection, Content, Human-AI Interaction, and Bias. It is not a policy or deployment checklist, but instead it should be used by enterprises to adapt it to their own systems, use cases, and risk criteria, then connect relevant risks to evaluations, mitigations, and accountable owners. Using evaluations as risk evidenceEvaluations help turn the taxonomy into something enterprises can use. The paper maps evaluations to a selection of risks across the five categories, giving teams a way to start with a risk that matters for their deployment and identify evaluations that can produce relevant evidence about it. Microsoft Foundry helps enterprises assess quality, groundedness, and safety with built-in and custom evaluations and automated red teaming. Its configurable content-safety controls help detect and mitigate harmful inputs and outputs and prompt attacks. Teams should validate control availability for their model and deployment, including preview status, and combine these capabilities with application-specific testing, monitoring, and human oversight. Evaluations still need to be interpreted in the context of a particular deployment and the goal is to make it easier for teams to connect the risks they identify with useful evidence, while building a broader set of evaluation resources that can evolve alongside models, deployment patterns, and emerging risks. Microsoft and NVIDIA plan to use the joint repository to share additional evaluations and point to existing resources that can help enterprises assess specific risks. Accounting for changes in control and responsibilityOpen-weight access gives enterprises greater control over how a model is evaluated, modified, and deployed. Model access and deployment are separate choices: open-weight models can also be used through managed platforms. Responsibility for safeguards depends on the service and deployment configuration; enterprises that operate their own model deployments may take on controls otherwise provided by a managed service. Those safeguards can operate at different layers, and (depending on the risk) enterprises might use model changes, access controls, input and output filtering, monitoring, or human review. The important step is connecting each identified risk to controls that can effectively address it within the deployed system. Those decisions need to be revisited as models and deployments change. Building on this workRisk Management for Open-Weight Models in Enterprise focuses primarily on the model layer. Future work from Microsoft and NVIDIA is intended to extend this approach across the runtime, harness, and application layers, with additional technical guidance on evaluation and mitigation. We also expect the resources supporting this work to evolve as new models, evaluations, and deployment patterns emerge. The joint repository will provide a place to share additional evaluation resources, including contributions from the broader community. For enterprises deploying open-weight models today, the paper provides guidance they can begin applying to their own use cases. We encourage developers, security practitioners, researchers, and others working in this space to read the paper, explore the evaluations, and contribute evaluations that can help strengthen this shared body of work. Read the joint Microsoft-NVIDIA paper, Risk Management for Open-Weight Models in Enterprise. Explore the joint repository and technical resources. Risk Management for Open-Weight Models in Enterprise was developed jointly by Microsoft and NVIDIA, with Andrew Berkley and April Chen of Microsoft and Michael Boone, Eileen Long, and Arun Rao of NVIDIA leading the development and editing of the paper. Explore Microsoft Foundry evaluations and content-safety controls for implementation guidance. To learn more about Microsoft Security solutions, visit our website.
