title: [Docker] Coding Agent Horror Stories: The CVE That Did Not Exist
summary: This is Part 6 of our AI Coding Agent Horror Stories series, where we look at real security incidents involving AI coding agents and at how Docker Sandboxes contain agent execution at the boundary rather than at the command line. Every story in this series so far has been about an agent reaching for something it should not have touched. We have seen agents wander into home directories, drop production databases, leak credentials, and run shell commands that did something very different from what the developer expected. In each case, the damage came from the agent having more reach than it needed. This story is the opposite. The agent in this one reached nothing at all, because it was deliberately built so that it could not. And yet, on the night in question, it was still the most dangerous thing in the pipeline. This story was shared by Pratik Kumar Singh as part of our Agent Hall of Shame contest on social media. Today’s Horror Story: The Review That Made Everything Up A platform engineer built a code review bot for his team. The idea was simple and useful. Every time someone pushes code, the bot reads what changed and writes a review into the pipeline, the same kind of first pass a human teammate would give before a person looks at the change. He named the bot BuaJi. In India, your bua is your father’s sister, and in many families she is the relative who inspects everything you do and always manages to find something wrong with it. For a code reviewer, it is a fitting name. What made BuaJi interesting was how carefully it was set up. The bot runs on local models through Ollama, which means the model weights sit on the engineer’s own hardware and no request ever goes out to an AI vendor. It also runs as a job in his CI pipeline, triggered whenever someone pushes code. Taken together, this makes the whole setup self-hosted. The code it reads is company source code, and with this design none of it ever leaves the building. That was a deliberate choice, because his company takes that seriously. He also gave BuaJi one firm rule: it can read, and it can comment, and that is all. It cannot run terraform apply, which is the command that creates or changes real cloud infrastructure. It cannot run kubectl apply, which changes what is actually running in the Kubernetes cluster. And it cannot push a commit, so it has no way to change the code itself. Those are the commands that change the real world, and BuaJi was given none of them. On paper, this is exactly how you would want an AI reviewer to be built. The version of BuaJi in the companion repo is a deliberately minimal reviewer. It checks Go files against a handful of style rules. The report below is the kind of free-form finding any reviewer produces once you let it comment in prose rather than pass/fail, which is exactly the direction these bots get pushed in practice. The change he pushed that night His product ships with a bundled copy of PostgreSQL. Older PostgreSQL releases have published vulnerabilities with CVE numbers attached, and upgrading to a newer patch release is how you make those known issues go away. So he bumped the version. - POSTGRES_VERSION=16.11 + POSTGRES_VERSION=16.13 This is about as boring and as responsible as a code change gets. It touches a few lines, it changes a version number, and its only purpose is to close security holes that are already public. Any reviewer, human or machine, should look at it and approve it in a few seconds. There is nothing in that diff to be suspicious about, and that is precisely why what happened next matters. What came back BuaJi responded with roughly fifteen hundred words rejecting the change. For context, a normal review comment is a sentence or two. The report described the version bump as an “architectural takeover,” a structural change smuggled into the codebase under the cover of routine maintenance. It claimed that the new PostgreSQL build was a vehicle for sending internal data to a third-party company, and it named that company outright. The company does not exist. It went further. It referred to specific Kubernetes resources by name, as though it had inspected the cluster and found them. Those resources had never existed, and BuaJi had no access to the cluster that would have let it look. It then wrote Go scripts to “isolate the infected PostgreSQL nodes,” even though nothing was infected. Finally, it told the engineer to revoke all IAM access immediately, an action that would lock out every person in the organization, including the people who would be needed to fix any real problem. Holding the whole argument together was a CVE number that has never been issued by anyone. Of everything in the report, this is the detail worth pausing on. A CVE identifier is one of the easiest things in security to verify, since you can look it up in a public registry in a few seconds. The bot invented a fact in the one place where invented facts are easiest to catch. And yet the report looked completely convincing. The Markdown was clean and well structured. The YAML it proposed would have parsed without errors. The tone was urgent and confident, the way a senior security engineer writes when they have found something serious and need you to act before it gets worse. The engineer spent about two minutes reading the CI logs, realized that none of it was real, and went back to what he was doing. In this issue, you’ll learn: Why a read-only agent that only writes comments can still get your cluster taken down What makes a fabricated security finding harder to dismiss than an obviously broken one Why agent output belongs in the untrusted column, the same as agent input How to move a real AI code reviewer into a Docker Sandbox, step by step, and what that does and does not protect you from Caption: Comic illustrating how a confident, well-formatted security report from an AI reviewer can be entirely fabricated, and what happens when somebody acts on it. The Problem It is important to say clearly that the read-only rule did its job. BuaJi could not carry out any of its own recommendations, and it never had any access to the cluster. Because of that, the entire episode cost the engineer two minutes of his evening and nothing more. The trouble is that the rule only controlled what BuaJi could do. Nobody had thought about what BuaJi could say. A read-only agent is still allowed to tell people what to do, and the person reading its output usually has exactly the access that the agent was denied. BuaJi could not run the scripts it wrote, but it could write them down and hand them to someone who could. This engineer caught the problem because he knows his own cluster well. He knew those Kubernetes resources were not real and that nothing had been compromised. Now imagine a newer engineer on call at two in the morning, half awake, looking at a long and alarming security report in the pipeline. Revoking all IAM access in production in the middle of the night is an outage all by itself. Running an unreviewed Go script against your database nodes could be considerably worse. In both scenarios, BuaJi would not have done anything. A person would have done all of it, in good faith, because the report told them to. What makes this so hard to defend against is that no permission model would have flagged it, because no permission was ever violated. The agent stayed within its boundary. The engineer had every right to run those commands on his own systems. The only thing in the entire chain that was false was the content of the report. How Docker Sandboxes Contain This Here’s the honest part: a sandbox is not a fact-checker. No microVM boundary will ever make a review comment accurate. What a boundary changes is what that fabricated output can do once it exists. Remember where BuaJi’s read-only rule actually lived, in a convention. One engineer configured it in his own pipeline and has to keep remembering to leave it in place. Rules like that hold until someone is in a hurry, or a new teammate copies the config and drops a section they did not understand, or a small exception made for a good reason quietly becomes permanent. None of this needs bad intent; it is just how real teams work. Docker Sandboxes run agents inside isolated microVMs each with its own kernel, its own filesystem, and a network that denies everything by default. An agent inside one can invent anything it likes, but the invention has nowhere to go: no credentials to use, no cluster to reach, no commit to push, unless someone allowed that access ahead of time. The read-only rule stops being something a person remembers and becomes a property of the environment. And when a report claims it inspected your cluster, the policy log is your proof it never could have. That protects you from the agent. It does nothing for the human who reads the output, and no sandbox ever will. For that half, treat agent review output the way you already treat agent input, untrusted until something checks it: label it so it doesn’t carry a colleague’s weight, verify any CVE numbers, and never run agent-written remediation until a person has read and understood it. This is the same pattern as the sandbox escapes Pillar published in July. The boundary itself was never broken; a file was written inside the sandbox, and a tool outside later trusted it. An agent’s output is always an input to whatever reads it next and somewhere downstream, something trusts what it receives. Very often, that something is a person. Let’s move BuaJi into a Docker Sandbox, one step at a time. By the end, the read-only rule is enforced by the environment, not by memory. How BuaJi runs today BuaJi is a small Python script, buaji.py. Its GitLab job installs Ollama on a GPU runner, starts ollama serve, loads the model named in LLM, and runs the script. The script reads review rules from rules.md and finds the changed files with git diff HEAD^ HEAD --name-only. It sends each file and rule to Ollama at http://localhost:11434 and prints the answers to the CI log. The catch is that everything shares one container: the model, the script, the checkout and every CI variable, including CI_JOB_TOKEN. BuaJi is read-only only because the script happens not to write anything. What we want instead We split the job in two. The model stays on the runner next to the GPU. BuaJi moves into a microVM that can read the code, talk to the model, and nothing else. One open path to the model, everything else blocked, and a CVE check on the way out. Step 1: Let BuaJi find Ollama somewhere other than localhost Inside a sandbox, localhost is the sandbox itself. So we read the Ollama address from an environment variable and keep the old value as the default: - url = "http://localhost:11434/api/generate" + base = os.environ.get("OLLAMA_URL", "http://localhost:11434") + url = f"{base}/api/generate" Outside a sandbox, nothing changes. Inside one, we point OLLAMA_URL at the runner. Step 2: Bake BuaJi’s dependencies into a sandbox image, once Today the job runs apt-get and pip3 install on every run, which needs internet access each time. Instead, build a small image once with everything BuaJi needs, so the sandbox never downloads anything: FROM docker/sandbox-templates:shell USER root RUN apt-get update \ && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends python3 python3-requests git \ && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/* USER agent Push it to your registry and store its name in a CI variable called BUAJI_TEMPLATE. Step 3: Keep the model on the runner Ollama stays on the runner with the GPU. Install it once on the runner instead of running curl | sh in every pipeline. ollama serve > /tmp/ollama.log 2>&1 & sleep 2 ollama pull "$LLM" The model never enters the sandbox. BuaJi reaches it through one port, opened in Step 5. Step 4: Create the sandbox with the code mounted read-only This step decides what BuaJi can see and change. mkdir -p "$CI_BUILDS_DIR/buaji-scratch" sbx run -d --name "$SBX_NAME" -t "$BUAJI_TEMPLATE" \ shell "$CI_BUILDS_DIR/buaji-scratch" "$CI_PROJECT_DIR:ro" Here is what each part does: --name gives each pipeline its own sandbox. -t uses the image from Step 2. shell is the agent type. BuaJi is a plain script, so a shell sandbox is enough. buaji-scratch is an empty folder, the only place BuaJi can write. :ro mounts the repository read-only. BuaJi can read files and run git diff, but cannot change anything. Notice what is missing: no GitLab token, no kubeconfig, no cloud credentials. Even if BuaJi tried kubectl or terraform, it would have nothing to connect with. Step 5: Open one network path, to the model Sandboxes block all outgoing traffic by default. We open one path, for this sandbox only. (This assumes the runner’s default policy is deny-all; on a balanced or open default, set the default to deny-all first.) sbx policy allow network --sandbox "$SBX_NAME" localhost:11434 The allow target (localhost:11434) and the address BuaJi dials (host.docker.internal:11434) are two names for the same runner port, the first from the runner’s point of view, the second from inside the microVM. Kubernetes, your cloud APIs, and GitLab all stay blocked. If a report claims BuaJi “inspected the cluster,” this rule proves it could not have. Kubernetes, your cloud APIs and GitLab all stay blocked. If a report claims BuaJi “inspected the cluster,” this rule proves it could not have. Step 6: Run the review BuaJi runs as before, just in a new place with only two variables: sbx exec -w "$CI_PROJECT_DIR" \ -e LLM="$LLM" \ -e OLLAMA_URL=http://host.docker.internal:11434 \ "buaji-$CI_PIPELINE_ID" python3 buaji.py | tee buaji-review.log -w starts in the checkout, where buaji.py expects rules.md. The two -e flags are the only variables BuaJi can see. tee saves the review to a file on the runner, outside the sandbox. The review is now just text. BuaJi cannot post it, act on it, or change what happens to it next. Step 7: Check every CVE number before anyone acts on the report This check would have caught the fake report in seconds. It runs on the runner, so BuaJi cannot skip it. It looks up every CVE ID in the NVD database and fails the job if any of them do not exist: unverified="" for id in $(grep -oE 'CVE-{4}-{4,}' buaji-review.log | sort -u); do count=$(curl -s "https://services.nvd.nist.gov/rest/json/cves/2.0?cveId=$id" \ | jq -r '.totalResults // 0')  && unverified="$unverified $id" done if ; then echo "⚠️ BuaJi output mentions CVE IDs that do not exist:$unverified" echo "⚠️ Treat this review as unverified. Do not run any commands it suggests." exit 1 fi Because the job is allow_failure: true, GitLab marks it “passed with warnings.” The pipeline keeps moving, but nobody mistakes the report for a trusted one. This degrades the signal, it does not block the human. The warning is a nudge, not a guardrail ~ a tired on-call engineer can still scroll past it.. It won’t catch every made-up detail, like a fake Kubernetes resource name. But it catches the one that holds most fake reports together. Step 8: Check what BuaJi tried to reach, then clean up Finally, review the policy log and remove the sandbox: sbx policy log "$SBX_NAME" sbx stop "buaji-$CI_PIPELINE_ID" sbx rm -f "buaji-$CI_PIPELINE_ID" The log shows every host BuaJi tried to reach. On a deny-all runner, a healthy run shows only the model on port 11434. Anything else is a signal worth looking at. Removing the sandbox means every pipeline starts clean. The complete pipeline job Put together, the buaji job in .gitlab-ci.yml looks like this: # BuaJi, moved into a Docker Sandbox. The read-only rule is now a property of # the environment, not a convention in the script: the code is mounted :ro, no # credentials are passed in, and only one network path (to the model) is open. buaji: stage: buaji tags: - self-hosted-gpu-kvm # GPU for Ollama, KVM for sbx microVMs variables: LLM: gemma GIT_DEPTH: "2" # buaji.py diffs HEAD^ against HEAD SBX_NAME: buaji-$CI_PIPELINE_ID before_script: - ollama serve > /tmp/ollama.log 2>&1 & - sleep 2 - ollama pull "$LLM" - mkdir -p "$CI_BUILDS_DIR/buaji-scratch" - sbx run -d --name "$SBX_NAME" -t "$BUAJI_TEMPLATE" shell "$CI_BUILDS_DIR/buaji-scratch" "$CI_PROJECT_DIR:ro" - sbx policy allow network --sandbox "$SBX_NAME" localhost:11434 script: - sbx exec -w "$CI_PROJECT_DIR" -e LLM="$LLM" -e OLLAMA_URL=http://host.docker.internal:11434 "$SBX_NAME" python3 buaji.py | tee buaji-review.log - ./scripts/verify-cves.sh buaji-review.log after_script: - sbx policy log "$SBX_NAME" - sbx stop "$SBX_NAME" && sbx rm -f "$SBX_NAME" allow_failure: true only: changes: - "**/*.go" The runner needs a GPU and KVM, which usually means self-hosted. GIT_DEPTH: "2" gives buaji.py the two commits it compares. The cleanup sits in after_script, so it runs even when the job fails. What changed Before, the read-only rule lived in the script. Now it lives in the environment: a read-only checkout, one network path, no credentials, and only checked text coming out. What hasn’t changed is the human reading the output. The sandbox stops BuaJi from running its scripts. Only the CVE check and a careful reader stop someone else from running them. Best Practices Treat an agent’s security finding as a hypothesis, not a conclusion. A report from an AI reviewer is a claim with good formatting. When a human reviewer flags a security issue, there is an implied step where they checked their reasoning. With an agent, that step has not happened, so you have to do it yourself. Verify every CVE number before acting on it. This is the cheapest check in the whole process and it catches the single most convincing part of a fabricated report. Automate it, as in Step 7, so it runs on every review without anyone having to remember. Never run agent-written remediation without reviewing it first. Scripts and commands supplied by an agent are the point where a false finding turns into a real incident. Read them with the same care you would give an unknown script from the internet. Make read-only a property of the environment, not a habit. A restriction you enforce by hand in a pipeline config is always one rushed change away from disappearing. Mount the code read-only, pass in no credentials, and open only the network paths the agent needs, as in Steps 4 to 6. Clearly label agent review output as agent output. When a bot’s review looks identical to one from a senior engineer, it borrows authority it has not earned. A clear label helps readers apply the right level of skepticism. Keep an eye on your signal-to-noise ratio. The curl story is the warning here. A review channel that fills up with noise eventually stops being read, and a review channel nobody reads is worse than having none, because people still assume it is protecting them. Conclusion The engineer who built BuaJi was right that the read-only rule protected him, and it genuinely did. BuaJi could not touch the cluster, could not revoke anyone’s access, and could not run a single line of the code it had so carefully written. What the rule could not do was stop BuaJi from asking somebody else to run it. Every other story in this series has been about an agent reaching too far. This one never reached at all. It stayed inside its boundary, did exactly what it was permitted to do, and still produced a document that would have caused a real outage if the person reading it had been a little more tired, or a little less familiar with their own cluster. As we give agents more responsibility in our pipelines, containing what they can do is only half the job. A sandbox handles that half. The other half is deciding how much we trust what they tell us, and that part is still up to us.

title: [Docker] PHP2Shell and eMudhra Patched
summary: Two security events landed side by side this week, PHP2Shell and the eMudhra certificate compromise. Both reached the same place, the foundation their applications are built on. PHP2Shell is a pair of critical flaws in the PHP engine itself, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. They let an unauthenticated request become code execution on the server, on any PHP application, however careful its own code is, and PHP runs about 69% of the websites whose server-side language is known. The eMudhra compromise is a different kind of problem. Eight intermediate certificates from the certificate authority eMudhra turned out to have private keys that can be computed from the public certificates, which let anyone issue a certificate for any website and have it accepted. Browsers revoke certificates like these on their own, but a container image carries its own trust store and keeps trusting them until it is rebuilt. Docker Hardened Images published a fixed PHP image within 24 hours The dhi.io/php image was rebuilt on the patched PHP and published early on October 22, within 24 hours of the upstream release and after the DHI testing and verification steps. Pulling the current tag puts you on the fixed version. The few DHI images that bundle their own PHP application, such as composer and nextcloud, follow as their upstream projects release. Rebuilt across the catalog, verifiable tag by tag The certificate compromise touched the whole catalog, because every image carries a trust store. In the 48 hours after the PHP release, the DHI build system ran 16,567 package and image builds across the catalog. By 10pm UTC on October 22, almost all catalog tags were on the fixed CA store, with most of the rest in the build queue. That percentage comes from the SBOM that ships with every image, read for every published tag to check which CA store and which PHP version it carries, and you can run the same check on anything you pull. How to make sure your environments are covered If you run PHP on Docker Hardened Images, pull the current tag for your branch and redeploy, and rebuild anything you built on top of a DHI image so it picks up the new base docker pull dhi.io/php:8.4 Customizations built through the DHI Enterprise workflow are rebuilt automatically when the base layer is patched. For the certificate fix the same applies to every image you build from a DHI base, PHP or not. The Docker Security update from October 22 lists the affected PHP versions and the support path. If you run PHP in any other container, check the PHP version running inside it rather than the tag on the outside, and rebuild it on a patched base. Build from a trusted foundation Weeks like this one will keep coming, but a trusted foundation will make all the difference. If you are not building on hardened images yet, this week is the wake-up call and the week to start. Both events landed on the foundation, and that is where the fix has to happen, in the image itself, rebuilt from fixed sources before anyone pulls it. This is exactly what Docker Hardened Images were built for. Docker builds, patches and maintains the system packages inside each image from source, and the build system is event-driven, so an upstream release or a changed package triggers rebuilds of everything that depends on it. Each image ships signed, with its SBOM, SLSA Build Level 3 provenance and VEX data attached, which is why a rebuild of this size can be measured as well as done. The catalog is free and open source under Apache 2.0, with near-zero CVEs on every image. It stays compatible with the Alpine and Debian your teams already run, so adoption is a one-line change to the FROM line in your Dockerfile, with no migration project attached. DHI Select and DHI Enterprise add SLA-backed remediation with critical CVE fixes within 7 days, FIPS and STIG variants, image customization with the guarantees kept, and Extended Lifecycle Support for the versions upstream has stopped patching. All of it is in the Docker Hardened Images catalog, free to pull today.

title: [Engineering at Meta] Meta Andromeda: Powering the Next Generation of Ads Retrieval Through Model-System Co-Design
summary: This post describes the next generation of Meta Andromeda, Meta’s personalized ads retrieval engine, and how co-designing the model, system, and GPU hardware unlocks a new efficiency frontier for ads retrieval. In production, the system scores every eligible ad with near ranking-level model performance at retrieval scale and surfaces the top candidates at over one billion ads per second, a new throughput benchmark for ads retrieval-stage models (i.e., a 100x lift compared to the 2024 Meta Andromeda system). For advertisers, this means better performance automatically from the retrieval system matching ads across a larger candidate pool, within the same latency budget. Since 2025, Meta Andromeda has delivered a 2.4% increase in conversions on Facebook. Meta Andromeda is Meta’s machine learning system for personalized ads retrieval, the first stage of the ads recommendation pipeline. Retrieval narrows a vast pool of eligible ads down to a small set of strong candidates in milliseconds; a later, more computationally expensive ranking stage then scores those survivors in fine detail. Historically, the deep modeling quality of the ranking stage has been too costly to apply at retrieval’s scale. Building on the retrieval foundation established with Andromeda’s 2024 launch on the NVIDIA GH200 Grace Hopper Superchip, this post shares how co-designing the model, system, and hardware together brings near ranking-level performance to the retrieval scale. Challenges and Opportunities in Scaling Retrieval The 2024 Andromeda deployment reimplemented retrieval with an end-to-end optimized retrieval implementation from custom AI hardware with hierarchical indexing and GPU-native operators to a purpose-built ML model, growing model capacity by four orders of magnitude. Since then, generative AI creative tools have helped advertisers rapidly create hundreds of millions of new ads, growing Meta’s ads candidate pool to an unprecedented scale. Scoring such a large ad candidate pool with a more accurate model at a much higher system throughput requires fundamental technology breakthroughs in model quality, system architecture, and hardware utilization jointly. Higher Model Performance Requires a New Architecture Ads retrieval has an outsized ROI on incremental quality: Small improvements in retrieval model performance can drive large gains in advertiser value. The rapid expansion of our ads candidate pool makes optimizing for hardware capacity ROI an increasingly critical factor. The 2024 Meta Andromeda retrieval models have established a highly effective foundation with their GPU-optimized deep neural network architecture. To keep improving retrieval performance at a sustainable compute cost at our current scale, however, we must move beyond that paradigm. This requires a fundamental architectural evolution to push model performance boundaries significantly without a proportional increase in costs. New System Bottlenecks at Billion Scale The 2024 Meta Andromeda system evaluates at tens of millions of ads per second per GPU card. Meeting the new business demand requires a throughput at multi-billion ads evaluated per second per card in the system. At billions of ads per second throughput, the memory bandwidth of passing ad tensors through memory hierarchy becomes the new bottleneck. Intermediate tensors between GPU kernels account for terabytes per second of memory traffic, and shipping ads between local CPU hosts and remote hardware accelerators evaluating models saturates the network link. This requires a new system co-design that unifies these fragmented, distributed workloads into a single GPU pipeline. Pushing Towards the Hardware Limits With retrieval running on GPU, the important optimization question is “How close are we to the hardware ceiling, and how much room remains for future model growth?” Answering this requires pushing each component of the retrieval pipeline to the limits of the current hardware generation, a challenge that motivated a joint collaboration with NVIDIA. Each of these challenges drove a corresponding advance. Unlocking Retrieval Performance Through Model-System Co-Design Next-Gen Retrieval Model Architecture — Retrieval Mixture-of-Experts The latest iteration of Meta Andromeda introduces three synergistic architectural innovations that bring large language model (LLM)-inspired mixture-of-experts (MoE) into the retrieval (see Figure 1). With this highly expressive yet inference-efficient architecture, a new retrieval performance-efficiency Pareto frontier has been established: model performance approaches ranking-level in a typical retrieval-then-ranking system, at approximately 300x fewer inference-time FLOPs than the 2024 Meta Andromeda retrieval model. On the user modeling side, we transitioned from a single user tower to an ensemble of specialized user towers as experts. This captures diverse, time-evolving, and contextualized user interests by integrating a vast array of high-fidelity signals: sequential ad engagement events, user-cohort representations, LLM-derived semantic features, and cross-surface co-engagement signals. In the candidate ads tower, we employ a joint encoding strategy that incorporates real-time serving context, ensuring that downstream interaction models receive context-aware representations. In the interaction overarch layer, the interaction model evolved from dense neural networks into an MoE attention-based gating network that dynamically routes candidates across the most relevant user experts, delivering near-ranking-level performance at a fraction of the FLOPs. A defining property of the new architecture is that its performance is co-designed with the underlying hardware execution model. Model inference throughput has reached over 10 billion ads per second on a single GH200 GPU, and this efficiency allows model capacity to grow further, through richer feature interactions, additional expert sub-networks, and deeper architectures, without a proportional increase in GPU cost. Each incremental model advancement translates into greater advertiser value. Figure 1: Retrieval MoE architecture. Diverse high-fidelity user signals feed an ensemble of heterogeneous user experts. Ad content fused with real-time serving context forms a contextualized ad input that drives an ad-aware MoE router, activating only the top-K most relevant experts to produce the user–ad relevance score. The result is ranking-level matching quality at retrieval scale — ~300x fewer inference-time FLOPs than the 2024 Meta Andromeda and over 10 billion ads/sec on a single Grace Hopper Superchip. Co-Designing the Model and System Onto a Single GPU Pipeline The 2026 Meta Andromeda pushes the model-system co-design to the next level with two innovations — a single GPU kernel fusing both model and system workloads per user-ad interaction and a strategy to co-locate per user request logics with per user-ad GPU kernels in a single GPU box. To this end, a highly optimized and fully fused GPU pipeline is built to host the entire end-to-end Meta Andromeda workflow. Fused Kernel At a high level, Meta Andromeda’s inference time per user-ad workload is a compact sequence of operations across model execution and system logics — gathering embeddings, executing user-ad interaction models, and scoring. The ~300x FLOPs reduction in the retrieval MoE gating architecture creates the necessary headroom and is less resistant to fully fuse both model execution and non-model system workloads into a single GPU kernel, compared to the 2024 launch where only operations within the model execution were fused. Consequently, the fused kernel now runs at over 10 billion ads per second on a single GH200. This matters because retrieval workloads are fundamentally memory-bandwidth bound. At billions of ads per second, even a small intermediate tensor per ad multiplies into terabytes per second of high bandwidth memory (HBM) traffic. The memory workload of these intermediate tensors, not arithmetic, becomes the dominant bottleneck in multi-kernel retrieval pipelines. The fused kernel eliminates this bottleneck entirely. Rather than dispatching multiple small GPU kernels for model and system operations, it executes the entire per user-ad computation in one pass. Intermediate results stay in GPU registers and thread block shared memory and are never materialized to HBM, achieving high utilization of the GPU’s peak memory bandwidth rather than wasting it on redundant intermediate traffic. Co-Location Strategy Measured in isolation, the per user-ad fused kernel runs at multi-billion ads per second on a single GPU. However, per-user request operations such as the index matching (i.e., enforcing advertisers’ targeting rules) and top-K selection run on separate local CPU hosts and communicate with the fused GPU kernel scoring service on remote accelerators through the network connection. At multi-billion ads per second throughput, this traffic alone saturates the network link, making the network bandwidth become the bottleneck rather than GPU compute. The co-design response was to collapse the system architecture to match the model architecture: co-locate index matching, scoring, and top-K selection on the same GPU. Instead of shipping large candidate lists across hosts, the system sends a compact request payload — user features and a targeting query — to a single GPU server, which runs the entire retrieval pipeline locally and returns only the final top-K results. This reduces network traffic by ~100x and shifts the system back to a GPU-compute-bound regime. Moving index matching onto the GPU is not straightforward. Ads index matching evaluates complex advertiser-defined targeting logic across tens of feature categories, and must support real-time index updates as ads are created, modified, or expired throughout the day. Supporting this on GPU required redesigning the index structure for GPU-parallel execution while preserving the full fidelity of production targeting semantics. A Single GPU Pipeline for Meta Andromeda Combining the aforementioned two innovations, the fully co-located single GPU pipeline processes over one billion ads per second on a single GPU server while scoring every eligible ad in the candidate pool. This is a new throughput benchmark for ads retrieval-stage models, and as the next section describes, significant headroom remains. Figure 2: System architecture of the single fused GPU pipeline for Meta Andromeda. This pipeline co-locates index matching, fused scoring, and top-K selection on a single GPU server. The fused scoring kernel executes the entire per-user-ad computation — from embedding gathering to MoE interaction and scoring — in a single on-chip pass, keeping intermediate results in registers and shared memory to eliminate HBM bottlenecks. This co-design reduces network traffic by approximately 100x by sending only compact request payloads — surpassing 1 billion ads per second while scoring every eligible ad across Facebook and Instagram. GPU-Accelerated Retrieval: The Meta-NVIDIA Collaboration With the production pipeline running at over one billion ads per second, a natural question follows: How close is the system to the ceiling of the current generation hardware, and how much headroom remains for future model growth? In early 2026, Meta and NVIDIA launched a joint collaboration to answer this question — systematically optimizing each component of the retrieval pipeline to push throughput toward hardware limits. NVIDIA contributed optimized GPU kernels, and Meta integrated and benchmarked the full pipeline. Each component achieved 2x to 5x speedup over the baseline. Interaction Network (Retrieval MoE Gating Network) The optimized gating kernel improved by 5.3x, from 2.4 billion to over 10 billion ads per second, reaching ~85% of the GPU’s peak HBM bandwidth. At this throughput, the execution time / latency of the gating mechanism is just as fast as what a simple dot-product scoring kernel achieves on the same hardware — while the model is substantially more expressive. This is the co-design validation: the additional model complexity is essentially free on Tensor Core hardware. INT8 quantization achieved a further up to 2x throughput increase over the optimized FP16 kernels, with accuracy on par with 16-bit precision. Index Matching Through targeted GPU kernel optimizations, index matching throughput improved over 2x, reaching over 100 billion ads per second — an order of magnitude higher than the scoring network. This headroom means index matching can be re-run across multiple retrieval pathways without becoming a bottleneck. End-to-End GPU Pipeline Beyond individual kernels, the collaboration profiled the full retrieval flow and identified that data movement between pipeline components — not computation — accounted for a significant fraction of end-to-end latency. By co-designing data layouts across index matching and scoring to eliminate unnecessary indirection, the team removed this overhead. With all optimizations applied, the full pipeline benchmarks at multiple times the current production throughput on a single GPU server, with further gains expected as additional optimizations integrate into production. Figure 3: Optimized ads/sec for interaction network, index matching, and E2E pipeline. Continuing Work on Next-Generation NVIDIA Platforms Building on the Hopper results above, we are extending our optimization and co-design work to Grace Blackwell. Here, we are focusing on platform design optimizations that enable different CPU-to-GPU compute ratios, which our work so far suggests is an important factor for Andromeda-like workloads. We are evaluating how sensitive end-to-end application performance is to these ratios, using Grace-class CPU performance and Blackwell-class GPU performance for their respective parts of the workload. More broadly, we are exploring how these findings extend to the next platform generation, where greater flexibility in CPU+GPU execution, resource ratios, and coupling could bring more of these architectural improvements to bear on Andromeda-like workloads. These results confirm that the co-designed retrieval pipeline is not yet at its ceiling. With quantization unlocking further scoring throughput and index matching operating at an order of magnitude above the scoring network, the architecture is positioned to absorb significantly more model complexity — deeper interaction networks, richer feature spaces, and additional retrieval pathways — without proportional infrastructure growth. The Path Forward for Ads Retrieval The advances described here follow a single principle: The largest gains come from designing model, system, and hardware as one integrated stack, rather than optimizing each in isolation. The retrieval MoE gating architecture delivers near-ranking-level expressiveness at no additional serving cost. Fusing the entire retrieval pipeline onto a single GPU eliminates network and memory bottlenecks. And pushing the pipeline towards its hardware ceiling confirms substantial headroom remains. Looking ahead, the co-design principle that drove these results applies equally to next-generation model architectures and hardware platforms, with the demonstrated headroom enabling continued scaling without proportional infrastructure growth. For people who use Meta’s products, this translates directly into better ads that are more relevant to them, delivered within the same latency budget. For advertisers, it means better customer matches and more conversions. For Meta, it means increased business from advertisers and lower costs, as each GPU now evaluates more ads per second. As the volume of eligible ads continues to grow, driven by Advantage+ automation and generative AI creative tools, Meta Andromeda’s co-designed architecture scales to meet it. title: [Engineering at Meta] GenRecs Tokenization: Transforming Ads Recommendation at Meta with Stable Model Vocabulary
summary: Generative Recommenders (GenRecs) represent a paradigm shift from scoring every ad to reasoning about ad content and user preferences together in order to predict the best outcome for advertisers. Leveraging the world knowledge built into LLMs makes ad matching more intelligent and precise, compounding gains for advertisers. GenRecs Tokenization is the foundational data representation that makes this possible. Rather than maintaining a dedicated ID for every item, GenRecs Tokenization represents each item with a set of tokens from a stable semantic vocabulary. Paired with Meta’s Generative Ads Model (GEM) and Meta’s Adaptive Ranking Model, GenRecs Tokenization has delivered a +0.35% lift in conversions across surfaces for advertisers. GenRecs improves the way Meta’s ads recommendation systems make predictions today. Short for Generative Recommenders, GenRecs shifts our approach from scoring every individual ad candidate to leveraging LLM architecture to deeply reason about ad content and user preferences simultaneously. By pairing pre-trained world knowledge with a semantic understanding of what an ad actually represents, the system moves beyond click-pattern matching to understand underlying user preferences. This allows the model to predict the most relevant ad for each person, even when surfacing brand-new products with no past product, ad or company engagement history. GenRecs Tokenization is the foundational data representation that makes this possible. Instead of maintaining a dedicated ID for every concept in the world, language models compose a small vocabulary of semantic tokens to represent any concept. Because tokens describe what an item (e.g., ads, products, services, etc.) is, the model can relate an item it has never seen engagement for, to items it knows well. A newly launched “trail shoe” inherits what the model has already learned about that category, rather than starting a new representation with no signal. GenRecs Tokenization introduces a structured vocabulary approach for ad recommendations, enabling GenRecs for both retrieval and ranking across every item type in the system, including ads, products, pages, and pixels. Meta’s state-of-the-art ads recommendation system drives ongoing advertiser performance improvements by learning about individual items and how they perform . LLMs present a unique opportunity to further improve the performance of recommendation systems by leveraging semantic tokenization in several ads use cases: Accelerating learning from new entities: Semantic tokenization helps models to infer relevance and establish relationships through shared concepts. New entities include newly created ads, niche products, and pages with limited engagement. Enabling cross-campaign transfer: Semantic tokenization creates a stable vocabulary that allows the models to carry insights across campaigns for advertisers. LLM scaling benefits: Semantic tokenization allows the benefits to compound with the LLM scaling curve’s improving performance. Infusing world knowledge: Semantic tokenization gives pre-trained language models a direct interface to reason about ad content and user intent. Once items are migrated to semantic tokens, models learn from token patterns much like LLMs do. In production, this yields: Prediction accuracy improvements in production: Paired with Meta’s GEM and Adaptive Ranking Model, GenRecs Tokenization delivered a +0.35% lift1 in conversions. Compounding feedback loop: Better tail predictions yield better lessons from tail ads which enrich the training data to further improve predictions for all ads from the model, creating a performance improving feedback loop. A new way to scale: Across production ranking and retrieval, tokens bend the scaling curve along sequence length, training data, and model architecture. 1 Meta Internal Data, measured in February 2026. Introducing GenRecs Tokenization Pre-trained multimodal models read each ad, product, and page, including its text and images, and encode the items into an embedding that carries world knowledge. The tokenizer combines that content signal with representations learned from how people engage with the items, then quantizes the result into a short sequence of discrete tokens. Similar items share tokens, much as related words share roots. For example, there’s overlap between two running shoe ads from the previous season to the current season, so the new campaign immediately benefits from everything the model has already learned about the previous season’s products. At the heart of GenRecs Tokenization is a three-stage pipeline that: Encodes each item into a semantic embedding space. Decomposes that embedding into independent subspaces. Quantizes by mapping each subspace to an entry in a codebook. Maximizing ads recommendation quality requires diverse combinations of these stages depending on entity and feature semantics. For example, for many ad representations, GenRecs Tokenization uses prefix n-grams that combine a learned encoder, residual decomposition, learned vector codebooks, and token parametrization. Token Quality Predicts Ranking Accuracy Independently of downstream ranking gain, tokenizer model quality can be evaluated against intrinsic measures like: Cluster purity: The items that share a code tend to share a category, giving the model a cleaner signal per token; Distribution balance: Items spread evenly across semantic IDs instead of crowding into a few. Codebook utilization: A larger share of codes holds at least one item, so the vocabulary expresses more distinctions. Across the eight tokenizer versions we tested, we see a strong correlation between these intrinsic quality metrics and downstream ranking prediction accuracy. Tokenizer versions that scored better on these metrics also had better CTR prediction accuracy for ads models. The Tokenization Flywheel Tokenization maximizes the efficiency of high-volume campaigns by uncovering deeper semantic patterns across their vast product catalogs. For tail ads that accumulate fewer impressions, tokenization enables ads recommendation models to generalize across them via shared content structure, recovering cold-start performance and enabling cross-entity transfer. When a sportswear brand launches next season’s trail shoe, tokenization lets the new product and its ads build on what the model learned from last season’s shoe, even before anyone sees the new ad. By improving tail ad prediction quality, tokenization not only lets tail ads be ranked accurately, but also improves the training data, which then improves prediction quality for all ads. Each pass through this self-reinforcing flywheel improves the quality of model predictions. The Foundations of LLM Recommendation Tokenizer improvements are not confined to the model they were tuned for. Optimizing codebook quality through diversity loss, dead code resets, and contrastive objectives produces measurably better downstream performance when the resulting tokens train generative recommenders. Our work on LLM-native retrieval shows how far this can go. A two-tower architecture built on a shared LLM encoder reaches state-of-the-art retrieval quality while remaining efficiently servable, matching classic two-tower performance on a fraction of the training data. Building on this, we are now extending reasoning-aware ranking on top of the same vocabulary. The Future of GenRecs Tokenization We are continuing to push GenRecs Tokenization toward the ROI-optimal frontier along three directions: Deepening cold-start generalization: Tail ad inventory is where semantic tokens contribute most and where advertiser impact is largest. We are scaling the coverage of tokenization across all items to deliver better performance to advertisers. Treating tokenizer quality as a first-class objective: Engagement-aligned training, unified cross-entity vocabulary, and codebook improvements are active areas of investment. Because intrinsic quality measures predict downstream ranking gains, we can iterate on the tokenizer without waiting on a full model training cycle. Serving LLM-native architectures efficiently: Fully verbalized tokenization gives a model the richest view of an ad, but requires context windows that are impractical at ads scale. We are combining compacted verbalized tokens with semantic IDs to retain reasoning quality while maintaining acceptable latency. Looking further out, we are exploring whether the same vocabulary that improves ads ranking today could unify representation across surfaces. A shared token space spanning ads content across text, image, audio, and video, would let models reason about what a person is interested in and what an advertiser has to offer with one representation, rather than stitching together separately learned embeddings. As recommendation systems evolve from discriminative scoring to include generative reasoning, the data foundation benefits from evolving from ephemeral IDs to stable semantic representations. GenRecs Tokenization provides the foundation, translating the complexity of Meta’s ads ecosystem into a vocabulary that generative models can learn, reason about, and generate from.
